#9686. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features


Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

What is Canva?

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Who is Canva best suited for?

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

Free vs Pro vs Enterprise Pricing plan

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

Free plan Features

  • 250,000+ free templates
  • 100+ design types (social media posts, presentations, letters, and more)
  • Hundreds of thousands of free photos and graphics
  • Invite members to your team
  • Collaborate and comment in real-time
  • 5GB of cloud storage
  • Try Canva Pro for free for 30 days

Pro Plan Features 

  • Everything Free, has plus:
  • 100+ million premium and  stock photos, videos, audio, and graphics
  • 610,000+ premium and free templates with new designs daily
  • Access to Background Remover and Magic Resize
  •  Create a library of your brand or campaign's colors, logos, and fonts with up to 100 Brand Kits
  • Remove image backgrounds instantly with background remover
  • Resize designs infinitely with Magic Resize
  • Save designs as templates for your team to use
  • 100GB of cloud storage
  • Schedule social media content to 8 platforms

Enterprise Plan Features

  • Everything Pro has plus:
  • Establish your brand's visual identity with logos, colors and fonts across multiple Brand Kits
  • Control your team's access to apps, graphics, logos, colors and fonts with brand controls
  • Built-in workflows to get approval on your designs
  • Set which elements your team can edit and stay on brand with template locking
  • Unlimited Storage
  • Log in with single-sign on (SSO) and have access to 24/7 Enterprise-level support.

How to Use Canva?

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

Canva Sign Up

Designing with Canva



When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

 Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Templates



Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.


 Canva has a lot to choose from, so start with a specific search.if you want to create business card just search for it and you will see alot of templates to choose from

Elements

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.


To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

Photos

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.


When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

 When you subscribe to Canva Pro, you get access to a number of premium features, including the Background Remover. This feature allows you to remove the background from any stock photo in  library or any image you upload.

Text

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows). 

Canva Pro subscribers can choose from a large library of fonts on the Brand Kit or the Styles tab. Enterprise-level controls ensure that visual content remains on-brand, no matter how many people are working on it.

Audio

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Video

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab. 

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

Backgrounds

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

Styles


The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

Logos

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

Publishing with Canva

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro subscribers can create multiple post formats from one design. For example, you can start by designing an Instagram post, and Canva's Magic Resizer can resize it for other networks, Stories, Reels, and other formats.

Canva Pro subscribers can also use Canva’s Content Planner to post content on eight different accounts on Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack, and Tumblr.

Canva Team

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

Canva Print

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts. 

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

Canva Apps

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

Canva Pros and Cons

Pros:

  • A user-friendly interface
  • Canva is a great tool for people who want to create professional graphics but don’t have graphic design skills.
  • Hundreds of templates, so you'll never have to start from scratch.
  • Wide variety of templates to fit multiple uses
  • Branding kits to keep your team consistent with the brand colors and fonts
  • Creating visual content on the go
  • You can find royalty free images, audio, and video without having to subscribe to another service.

Cons:

  • Some professional templates are available for Pro user only
  • Advanced photo editing features like blurring or erasing a specific area are missing.
  • Some elements that fall outside of a design are tricky to retrieve.
  • Features (like Canva presentations) could use some improvement.
  • If you are a regular user of Adobe products, you might find Canva's features limited.
  • Prefers to work with vectors. Especially logos.
  • Expensive enterprise pricing

Conclusion

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. If you have any queries let me know in the comments section.

#9685. The Business Judgment Rule Does Not Judge the Business

Chief Strategy Officer | Board Dir. | AI | Org. & Ops. Effectiveness | Corp. Finance | Capital Markets | VC & PE | https://sanforddiday.com

Chief Strategy Officer | Board Dir. | AI | Org. & Ops. Effectiveness | Corp. Finance | Capital Markets | VC & PE | https://sanforddiday.com

Chief Strategy Officer | Board Dir. | AI | Org. & Ops. Effectiveness | Corp. Finance | Capital Markets | VC & PE | https://sanforddiday.com

Market Basket shows why strong results do not put a CEO beyond oversight, and why lawful board authority is not the same thing as business wisdom.

Strong operating results did not settle Market Basket's boardroom fight. On April 20, 2026, Vice Chancellor J. Travis Laster of the Delaware Court of Chancery upheld the suspension and subsequent firing of longtime president and CEO Arthur T. Demoulas, while acknowledging the company's operating success (DSM HoldCo). The central question was whether the directors acted in good faith in exercising their authority, not whether firing Demoulas was the best business choice.

The ruling separates authority to remove a CEO from the wisdom of that decision. This article and this series draw a broader governance lesson from that distinction: a board's job is to protect the company's enduring character and accountability, not just referee its machinery. The three-day trial addressed the narrower question of whether these directors acted lawfully (Moran; DSM HoldCo).

What Does the Business Judgment Rule Actually Protect?

The business judgment rule limits judicial second-guessing when it applies. In this case, Demoulas had to prove that a majority of the directors acted in bad faith. The court found that he failed to do so (DSM HoldCo). Laster took the case under submission on February 25, 2026, and issued his opinion on April 20. The outcome established that Demoulas had not met that burden, rather than that the board had chosen wisely. Honesty alone does not capture the rule's full requirements.

Market Basket's public story centers on low prices and loyal cashiers. In 2014, workers shut down stores for weeks to demand Demoulas's reinstatement after an earlier ouster by his cousins. The walkout made the chain a folk-hero story and ended in a $1.6 billion buyout that put Demoulas and his three sisters in sole control of the company (Chesto). Eleven years later, the boardroom fight pitted him against the sisters who had once helped bring him back. That history explains the public stakes; customer loyalty alone did not resolve the legal question.

Demoulas grew Market Basket into an operation generating roughly $8 billion in annual revenue and employing more than 30,000 people (Chesto). By any ordinary measure, he did his job well, and the court did not dispute that. Laster wrote that Demoulas "proved to be an excellent operator, but an imperious leader," adding that strong performance is "not the only dimension of a CEO's job" (DSM HoldCo).

The board's concerns extended beyond operating results. In August 2024, it gave Demoulas a five-item "Issues List" covering budgets, capital expenditure approvals, and succession, including rejecting automatic succession by his children. The opinion describes his failure to resolve those issues (DSM HoldCo). Reports of a possible walkout and boycott heightened the directors' concerns in spring 2025. They suspended him in May pending an outside investigation by Quinn Emanuel, then terminated him in September after unsuccessful mediation (DSM HoldCo; Solis). The investigation's conclusions supported the board's position. Those investigative conclusions and the court's findings represent separate parts of the record.

Two companies, DSM HoldCo and Demoulas Super Markets, brought the Section 225 action with directors Jay Hachigian, Steven Collins, and Michael Keyes to confirm the validity of Demoulas's removal. Demoulas counterclaimed that the directors breached their fiduciary duties by suspending and terminating him. He sought reinstatement as president and CEO (DSM HoldCo; Pelletiere and Boston 25 News Staff). At trial, he had to prove that a majority of the directors had acted in bad faith. He did not meet that burden. Laster rejected the claim that the directors were beholden to the sisters and found a rational basis for their concern about a repeat of 2014. The court upheld the removal (DSM HoldCo).

This case turns on a distinction between operating performance and governance cooperation, rather than a single verdict on a CEO. The two dimensions ask different questions. Collapsing them into one obscures what the court decided.

Operating performance covers revenue, growth, and customer loyalty, familiar subjects in shareholder letters. Governance cooperation asks different questions: whether management gives directors transparent information, plans succession honestly, and accepts that a board's authority to ask questions does not shrink as the business grows. Strong results and legitimate oversight address distinct responsibilities; neither cancels the other. The board, in turn, must exercise its authority for the company, not merely demand obedience.

Could the directors act independently of a powerful executive and obtain the information they needed to govern? Those are the two questions in the series' Independence and Information framework. In this dispute, their documentation began with unresolved issues in 2024 and continued through the May 2025 suspension pending investigation, the investigation itself, and unsuccessful mediation before termination. The court upheld their exercise of judgment on that record (DSM HoldCo). The documents supported the decision as evidence; the obligation to act in the company's interests remained.

The independence question starts with the family dispute. Outside status alone cannot establish a director's independence. Selection by one side of the family, by contrast, does not by itself prove bad faith. What matters is whether the directors exercised judgment for the company rather than serving a faction. The court rejected Demoulas's challenge on the record before it (DSM HoldCo).

None of this settles what Market Basket's culture or legacy required. Demoulas led a business with substantial employee and customer loyalty, and his supporters argue that the hands-on style they associate with "Artie T." helped sustain that success across roughly ninety stores. A spokesperson for Demoulas acknowledged that Delaware's deference to directors imposed high hurdles, but pointed to strong performance as evidence the company did not need fixing (Pelletiere and Boston 25 News Staff). That argument deserves a hearing. It is not a frivolous one.

The strongest objection concerns what removal would mean for the business. The directors could have authority to act without proving that firing Demoulas would preserve Market Basket's advantages better than a workable compromise. Strong results, meanwhile, could not put the CEO beyond oversight. The ruling resolves the legal challenge. It cannot show how the company would have fared under a different arrangement.

The unresolved business question leaves responsibilities intact on both sides. Strong operating results do not erase a board's oversight role. The board must exercise authority over management for the company, rather than treat control as an end in itself. Successful operations and legitimate oversight must coexist.

Section 225 supplied a focused procedure for determining whether Demoulas's removal was valid. The case moved from the September 2025 filing to the April 20, 2026 post-trial opinion in about seven months (DSM HoldCo; Vinson & Elkins). That pace gave this particular leadership dispute a prompt answer. The record also extended beyond the termination meeting: unresolved governance requests, an outside investigation, and unsuccessful mediation preceded the firing.

Ten days after the ruling, Market Basket named a former teenage bagger as its new president. Chuck Casassa, the operations director, joined the chain at fourteen in 1976. The April 30, 2026 announcement also marked the retirement of interim CEO Don Mulligan after more than four decades with the company, including 27 years as CFO (Riley). Separately, the board said the company was not for sale, would remain family-owned, and expected to work productively with Demoulas as a shareholder (Pelletiere and Boston 25 News Staff). Those statements describe the board's intentions. The long-term effects of its decision remain an open question.

The ruling gives family-company executives a clear answer to a recurring governance question: strong operating results do not put management beyond legitimate oversight. Performance is part of the job, not the whole job. Accountability matters too. Directors have a corresponding responsibility to exercise their authority on behalf of the company.

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

#9681. Claude Fable 5.2: Why Anthropic's Most Expensive Model Can End Up the Cheapest

Successful 18 years career track in IT and EdTech. Solid experience and knowledge of all business areas

Successful 18 years career track in IT and EdTech. Solid experience and knowledge of all business areas

Successful 18 years career track in IT and EdTech. Solid experience and knowledge of all business areas

Claude Fable 5.2 looks like a point release. It isn't. Here's what I think the model actually is, based on running Fable on real work: a different class of system that holds long tasks and keeps checking its own work; a model where the mode matters as much as the model itself; a model whose Max mode can do worse than Medium while costing five times more; and proof that you have to compare final results, not tokens.

My wife and I recently drove up to Napa, a wine region just north of San Francisco. On the way, I was talking with a friend, an entrepreneur. As always, the conversation turned to artificial intelligence and to the fact that I host ToTheMoon, an AI podcast from Silicon Valley. And, as always, we ran into the same thing. He said: "I use AI. We have different agents, we analyze our customers, our service runs on it."

I told him I'd give him the best advice of his life, at least when it comes to AI. Watch two ToTheMoon episodes where I break down the biggest AI trends, then rate yourself from 0 to 100 on how well you understand artificial intelligence. Right now you feel like a 60. Unless you're a deeply involved professional user, afterward you should feel like a zero.

By the way, when he said I understand AI pretty well, I told him I understand it at zero. Let me use Fable 5.2 to explain what I mean.

In November, Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2. It seems like a small update: 5.1 became 5.2. What's the difference? Next to it sits Opus 5.5, OpenAI has its own lineups, and you can get lost in all of it.

Even Anthropic's own prompting guide notes that, in its testing, Fable 5.2 at its lowest effort level scored close to what Fable 5.1 did at higher levels. But the main thing is that Fable is a system of a different class — a different class of work altogether. To understand it, you have to start with where it came from.

Anthropic has a model family called Mythos. It's not available to regular people: only to special companies and specially approved individuals. These models were originally built for security — cybersecurity and finding vulnerabilities. One of the best-known cases came in late spring: these models were used to analyze a large number of open-source systems and found more than 10,000 different bugs and errors.

But such a model can not only find vulnerabilities — it can create them too. That's why Mythos models are probably the most advanced weapon in the world today when it comes to cybercrime and software.

Fable is the part of that family that's available to people. Ask it to analyze your own software — a website, a homegrown CRM, a server at home — and find vulnerabilities, and it will surface a fairly large number of serious problems. It lets you close holes that human programmers could never close — not this quickly, not this far in advance, and not at this scale. I may get a pile of comments from programmers for this. But I'm a former programmer myself, I know a fair amount about building systems, and I don't believe a human was ever capable of that.

Over the summer, Fable made an incredible splash — and became the first model the US government officially blocked, after reports that it could supposedly be used to build various kinds of weapons, both cyberweapons and offline ones. In general, models at the Mythos level make it possible to create serious biological weapons too — and, at the same time, to make very serious discoveries in medicine. There are several versions of why Anthropic clashed with the US authorities, from politics to marketing, and I went through them in the full episode. The outcome: the model was unblocked and released again after several changes. Alongside Fable 5.2, Anthropic also released Mythos 5.2, still for verified organizations only.

Remember the arc: released, blocked, reopened — but with restrictions and limits. We'll come back to it.

I first tried Fable before the block. I was in Santa Barbara, my kids were swimming in the pool, and I launched Claude Code from my phone.

I was blown away by the quality of its work. For the first time, a system worked this seriously — not small stuff, but big, serious tasks. You just described the task by voice, and it knew your infrastructure, understood what you wanted, and carried the task through to the end. It held a long working cycle, which, as we know, matters a lot in development: keeping the context going, forward and deep.

Modern models don't work only within your single context. While it works on the main task, Fable 5.2 keeps double-checking itself and launching new sessions in parallel. You don't have just one session running — parallel sessions start up, and something is always moving.

Double-checking is one of the ideas I keep repeating from episode to episode: on every important answer, I tell the system, "check yourself." Now a strong model does it on its own as well. Anthropic's guide says that at its highest effort levels in agentic coding, Fable 5.2 used subagents to review its own work — something Fable 5.1 didn't do on the same tasks.

And in the future, the task will already be done, while the session keeps working. That's the essence. This technology is essentially already in Dots in ChatGPT — Dots, by the way, is incredible. A friend and I rented a house up north for five days to lock ourselves in and work. As soon as the Airbnb booking email hit my inbox, Dots messaged me five minutes later: "I want to point out that you have conflicts. Your daughter has a concert on Sunday, and a piano tuner is coming to your place on Monday." I never asked it to do that.

Imagine the same for your own affairs. You signed a contract, agreed to hold an event, got everything ready — and a week later the law changed. And the system tells you: "Just a reminder: the rules have changed, the price has changed." It's great when a system can keep working after you've finished a task. For now, Dots doesn't spend huge compute on this, so the monitoring is still relative.

Ask your family which version of ChatGPT they use. My wife has used it for three years and is one of its 50 million active users. Which model, which number? She doesn't know. Does she understand the modes? Unlikely. She has a $20 paid plan with Medium selected. I usually tease everyone who doesn't pick a version and tell them: "Turn it up."

But that's normal. You don't know how many megapixels your iPhone has either. What normal person would know that? Except that this has created insane confusion in the market, and it persists: Low, Medium, High, Extra High, Max, Ultra — and the modes differ from product to product.

Once again: there's the model, and there's the mode. To compare Fable and Opus and figure out which is better, you need to understand what task you're doing and which mode you're working in.

And here's the catch. On a simpler model or a lower mode, a task can take three hours — and end up only 30% solved, or not solved at all. Another mode can solve it in ten minutes, 100%. In the end, on a more powerful model whose tokens cost much more and burn faster, you can spend less actual money.

Now the part that breaks people's brains. Fable's Max mode, I believe, costs three and a half times as much as Medium. And Max can do the task worse — while spending five times more money.

You might wonder: how can better reasoning be worse? That's the whole point: it can launch unnecessary agents, go in the wrong direction, and start doing things you don't need right now. It's a known fact that Fable models can lose context, stop abruptly, wander off, and launch extra agents.

Interestingly, Anthropic's own overview of Fable 5.2 says that most of the capability gain is already present at High, gains above it are uneven, and Max is for measuring the model's ceiling and for the rare task where time and tokens don't matter. At lower levels, the model is more likely to stop before the work is done; at higher ones, it delegates to subagents more readily.

For contrast, here's my most expensive story. I think it was July, right when OpenAI released Sol. I gave ChatGPT a task and walked away, and it worked on it for two and a half days. When I came back, I said: "So, did you solve it? I think you're stuck." And it replied: "I'm still working on the first item." It simply burned about 10 billion of my tokens. Fable, by the way, has never spent anything close to that for me.

Still, my advice is this. If you're not running out of tokens, use the maximum modes: in most cases, the maximum mode will give you a better result. But it's important to remember that it can do worse — many experiments won't show you that.

Take the cases people share around the world — say, a system cloning a Shopify-level site. One model in one mode spent $300, another spent $900 on the same thing, or the other way around. And if you compare all these cases with each other, you won't see any correlation about what's cheaper or what's right.

If you're watching a blogger who lays out ultimate rules — which mode and which model to pick, how tokens get spent, claiming he has tested everything — that's a conditional truth. Even for him, the same task can play out differently today and the day after tomorrow: models change, you don't know which test group you landed in, which country you were in, what account you had — and whether you got lucky.

Even official benchmarks don't give a simple answer. In September, Opus 5.5 came out: on terminal-based tests — maybe not a super-important metric — it scored 66%, while Fable had 55%. And I had a big question. If Fable is a system capable of hacking anything, with a colossal level of data analysis and system building, then what is this Opus 5.5, released to everyone, that outperforms it? Or did they make Fable worse? Many people remember that Fable got worse in July. Then, about six weeks later, Fable 5.2 came out — and it wins at complex programming by a lot. And complex programming is essentially any automation. It wins by multiples.

Price per token is only half the equation, too. According to Anthropic's price list, Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens — 20% cheaper than Fable 5.1 and twice the price of Opus 5.5. But at one point on my $200 plan, Fable started eating all my tokens in four or five hours, and Fable 5.1 once ate my entire subscription allowance in two.

How can you even compare systems by tokens, when what you need to compare is the final result? You ask yourself: was the result achieved or not? And to figure out what works better, you have to run hundreds of different tasks, even the strangest ones.

If a task is routine, more or less small, or several different answers would work for you, you probably don't need Fable. In my view, Opus 5.5 is number one today for high-volume development, building business processes, and large-scale automation. At the same time, I remain a daily ChatGPT user — for chats and basic life tasks — and a Codex user. If you can afford two $100 plans, get ChatGPT for $100 and Anthropic for $100 — you'll feel a really strong effect.

Fable is like plugging a unique brain into a task. If you need the most thoroughly verified result with the highest final efficiency, Fable is very interesting:

A recent example. The other day I had one fairly complex task, and Opus 5.5 was working on it. Late at night, I switched it to Fable 5.2, because I didn't fully trust Opus. There was too much money riding on it.

An honest caveat. In my opinion, Fable definitely can't fully manage advertising on its own yet. But ad analysis — absolutely. And right now is a unique time, when you can squeeze a thousand times better ad setup out of Fable. Five years ago, no system existed that could squeeze out that kind of efficiency. A time will come when this is impossible to do — I guarantee it.

If you can't pay $200 every month, you can buy the $200 plan once and try to get something done with it. For organizing your finances, I specifically recommend Fable. It's worth at least understanding that a model this powerful exists.

That's the arc I mentioned: Fable was released, blocked, reopened — and then restrictions and limits came in. Most people, using free systems or a cheap subscription, don't even come close to having access to serious models. And to do the kind of things we're doing now, over time you'll have to pay tens of thousands of dollars. That's how it should be.

More than a year ago, Sam Altman described a very interesting case, and I think it's very viable. He said a time will come when you tell yourself, "I have $20,000 to solve this problem," hand it to AI, and it solves it. We're not there yet, because right now you pay after the fact: you can spend $20,000 and it won't even start the task, or it'll go the wrong way. Today, AI can't really plan its own spending.

But the logic itself is right. People come to me very often about starting a business. I tell them: "You shouldn't start a business. You can pay me $10,000 — I just gave you good advice, because you'll save a hundred." People aren't used to paying like that, but it's the right price. If you're putting $100,000–$200,000 into a business, and your chance of losing is about 80% from the start — and it usually is — then paying AI $5,000 to work through your problem is the right move.

People don't do this because they think in terms of expenses. They'd rather spend that $5,000 on a vacation, a hotel, a bag, or a couch than invest it in the right financial strategy for their household, a financial strategy for their business, or a marketing management system.

I often run into this exchange. "Who runs your ads?" "We do it ourselves." "But you don't know advertising." "Well, we can't hire anyone right now; our whole ad budget is $1,500." Then at least pay $300 for ad analysis by these AI systems and spend $1,200 on the ads. Actually, you don't even need to pay the $300: it's about 10% of a $200 plan.

I believe every ordinary person should now build business processes. Even my wife. Because in the near future, it will be less and less clear whom you can trust with a given task.

Right now you can still buy something without being manipulated and see something without being manipulated. But we're moving into a time when manipulation becomes far more serious than it is now. My kids are already growing up in an era of super-manipulation: there are incredibly many channels for influencing a person. And we're entering an era when artificial intelligence will truly know who you are. Everything before that was kindergarten.

I started saying this about fifteen years ago: I deeply disliked the market of deception in professional marketing. Marketers all said, "We know our customers, we've studied them, we've analyzed them." But that doesn't compare to what it means to know your customer the way artificial intelligence does now.

Back to the drive from Napa. I asked my friend what he uses. "I have a ChatGPT subscription, I use DeepSeek." And I think he said he has Claude Code. I asked, "How much is your most expensive subscription?" "Twenty dollars." That's it — zero, right away. And he's a businessman with millions of dollars in monthly revenue. Then I heard DeepSeek, and I immediately got bored.

How do you even measure how well someone understands AI? A surgeon has parameters: how many operations, how many hours of surgery, the longest operation, where they studied, whom they worked with. A pilot has flight hours, countries flown, tough situations, aircraft types. But assessing how well a person grasps AI for their life is very hard today.

Even the people who create AI — Sam Altman, Dario Amodei — understand it very strategically, as visionaries. But many of them would find it hard to grasp the newest use cases — unless they're fanatics who build systems and create use cases themselves every day. Judging by their interviews, most of them aren't fanatics of these systems. Yet we're used to trusting: if someone talks about AI and has a hundred billion dollars, everyone assumes they understand it. And having worked as a programmer for forty years doesn't mean you understand AI. I recently read a programmer with twenty years of experience writing that he doesn't want to and won't use AI because it harms the tech world.

So your task today is to figure out what level of development and perception of AI you're at, and to keep checking against it. If you care about your professional growth, your business, your education, and your future, honestly rate yourself from 0 to 100. The gap between those who truly use AI and everyone else is already cosmic. And it will be catastrophic — and you won't even notice when it happens.

Tell me in the comments what level you see in yourself. Do you know which model you're using and why you chose it? Have you tried Fable 5.2 or Opus 5.5?

Alexander Volchek is an entrepreneur and builder, a strategic advisor to 200+ startups and scale-ups, and the host of ToTheMoon, an independent AI media outlet from Silicon Valley. Episodes, breakdowns, and company dossiers: besolid.com/tothemoon. YouTube: @ToTheMoonTech.

#9680. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

#9679. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

#9678. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9677. AI Is Dividing Product Designers: Exploring vs. Building

Design Engineer at Matter Labs (creators of ZKsync and Prividium). Creator of DecentWealth, ScrollChess, and a few other apps.

Design Engineer at Matter Labs (creators of ZKsync and Prividium). Creator of DecentWealth, ScrollChess, and a few other apps.

Design Engineer at Matter Labs (creators of ZKsync and Prividium). Creator of DecentWealth, ScrollChess, and a few other apps.

In October, I attended PUSH UX in Munich, Europe's largest conference on product design and user experience, featuring speakers from Anthropic, Wise, Google, IKEA, n8n, and other prominent organizations. On my way home, I kept thinking about one recurring theme: product design teams are approaching AI from fundamentally different perspectives.

Some are cautiously experimenting with AI while trying to fit it into established processes. Others have already integrated it into their daily workflows, connecting research, prototyping, design, and code with fewer handoffs. The difference goes beyond tool adoption. It reflects how teams understand their work, organize collaboration, and measure product value.

Paulo Oliveira from IKEA highlighted a fundamental problem with the way organizations approach AI:

"Most efforts start with tools, copilots and automation, and mistake faster cycles for value. The result is a pile of pilots nobody adopted, and a lot of people wondering what happened to the work they were good at. The alternative: to build something that fits, lasts, and makes an organization better at what it already does well. That starts by refusing the AI first, AI everything instinct."

I think this captures one of the central challenges in product design today.

Adding AI to an existing workflow can make individual tasks faster without improving the product or the way a team operates. Organizations can accumulate tools and experiments while leaving the underlying processes unchanged.

Meaningful adoption starts with understanding where teams lose time, which handoffs create friction, and where AI can improve how products are researched, designed, built, and validated.

For years, product design and software development operated as distinct stages. Designers worked in Figma, documented interactions, prepared specifications, and handed their work to engineers for implementation. This division made sense when building and testing functional interfaces required substantial engineering resources. AI-assisted development is changing that relationship.

After years of designing fintech and blockchain-based products, I kept encountering the same limitation: I could design an experience without having full control over how it was implemented.

About a year ago, I started building websites and applications from scratch with AI tools. As I described in my previous Hackernoon article, Claude Code Finally Made Me an Engineer After 10 Years in Figma, my workflow shifted from almost entirely Figma to roughly 90% Claude Code.

Working closer to production code lets me build, test, and iterate on interfaces directly, with fewer handoffs between design and engineering.

For product teams, this opens up several possibilities:

This doesn't mean every designer needs to become a full-time software engineer. Deep specialization remains essential, particularly in complex products. However, designers can work closer to implementation and contribute beyond the traditional boundaries of their roles.

Another exciting development is how AI is changing prototyping. Think about how difficult it used to be to create an interactive prototype for a specific device, such as an Apple Watch or an in-car infotainment system. Even without writing production code, designers can now use AI to build interactive prototypes tailored to specific hardware and explore how their ideas work in real-world contexts.

As AI makes prototyping, coding, and exploring alternatives easier, the focus of design work is shifting toward decision-making and product quality. Understanding whether it solves the right problem, meets user needs, and works reliably requires experience and critical judgment.

This is where faster workflows can create lasting value. Teams have more opportunities to test assumptions, explore alternatives, and identify problems before committing significant resources to a solution. However, individual productivity gains aren't enough. Organizations need to connect design, engineering, and product teams around shared workflows, clear quality standards, and meaningful evaluation of AI-generated output.

I'm particularly interested in how this can shape an AI-first product culture. The goal is to encourage experimentation while maintaining the technical rigor, security, and reliability that deep tech products demand.

Many designers argue that AI-generated product experiences lack quality. Are they right? Sometimes. Can the results improve? Absolutely.

AI-assisted research and discovery can produce shallow or generic results, especially when designers rely on AI without applying their own expertise and critical judgment. The quality of the outcome depends on how thoughtfully people guide, evaluate, and refine the process. Julia Bastian from Alasco explored this challenge in a session on AI discovery slop, examining how to recognize and address low-quality AI-generated research and insights.

The PUSH UX conference reinforced how differently the design community is responding to AI. Some teams are still finding their footing, while others are already changing how they work. My own experience has made me more comfortable working across design, product strategy and engineering, but every team will need to find its own approach.

The important shift is to reconsider established workflows, explore where new capabilities can make a difference, and take greater ownership of business outcomes.

#9676. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9674. Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.
