#9673. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

 


Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

What is Sellfy?

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Features

Sellfy includes:

Online Store

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Product hosting

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Embed options

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Payments and security

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.


Marketing and analytics tools

The Sellfy platform includes marketing and analytics tools to help you manage your online store. You can send email product updates and collect newsletter subscribers through the platform. With Sellfy, you can also offer discount codes and product upsells, as well as create and track Facebook and Twitter ads for your store. The software's analytics dashboard will help you track your best-performing products, generated revenue, traffic channels, top locations, and overall store performance.

Integrations

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy Review: Pros and Cons

#9671. TETRA Wants to Reinvent the Database. Its Ambitions Go Much Further

Got Tech, Data, AI and Media, and not afraid to use them.

Got Tech, Data, AI and Media, and not afraid to use them.

Got Tech, Data, AI and Media, and not afraid to use them.

TETRA may be the most innovative startup you’ve never heard of. TETRA started as an attempt to make graph workloads faster and more efficient. It became something far more ambitious: a matrix-based data engine built on Collapsive Architecture that brings data representation, storage and query execution together.

Approaching TETRA as a graph database is a good way to get introduced to it. But TETRA is nothing short of a paradigm shift, and the impact goes well beyond graph.

Graph technology is special. It makes relationships between things explicit, revealing connections and context that conventional data models often leave hidden.

There is no shortage of graph technology these days. I know, because I’ve been working in the field for 20 years, and keeping track of it for the last 10 years. As AI moves from experimentation into real-world applications, organizations  are looking for ways to give LLMs context that is relevant, connected and grounded in their own knowledge.

At the same time, vibe coding has lowered the bar for creating software, and graph technology projects are proliferating. Some days it feels as though another one lands every time I open LinkedIn.

So when Kyle Mickey began posting about TETRA in March 2026, I initially filed it under “yet another graph database”. But the performance claims and, more importantly, the suggestion that the design was fundamentally different got my attention. I wanted to understand what was different, and whether the claims held up to scrutiny.

This is how this journey unfolded, where it goes next, and why rethinking infrastructure is a big deal whether you are into graph technology or not.

A disclosure before we go further: I am now a Strategic Advisor to TETRA. I came for the graph database and stayed for the vision. That affiliation is relevant context for readers, and it is also why I have tried to distinguish what is a part of the conversation, what TETRA has published, and what remains to be demonstrated in customer deployments.

Mickey, as he prefers to be called, studied English, psychology and the humanities, traveled with the idea of teaching English, then worked in health and human services before moving into technical writing and geophysics.

From there came software configuration, engineering, application development and operations, including more than a decade on AWS. He now builds from Costa Rica. It is not the usual database founder’s résumé, which may explain why he asks unusual questions.

The path to TETRA began with a practical problem: making LLM inference more efficient. Mickey was working on GPU kernels and thinking about how an LLM could become just another capability in an API stack, rather than a separate architectural universe.

As he read research on embeddings and the mathematics behind them, he kept encountering graph Laplacians and linear algebra. Work by Lorenzo Moriondo was one of the prompts that made him look more closely. One question stayed with him:

“Why would it be that embeddings are showing these same properties as a matrix, as a graph representation?”

Embeddings turn prompts into numerical representations that models can process. Mickey began to wonder whether the mathematical properties he saw in embeddings and model weights could also represent and query ordinary data.

If graphs can be represented as matrices, could a database use that representation too?

Mickey profiled existing databases and traced where they slowed down: the system would fetch information from memory or disk, then return to processing. He started hacking away trying to answer one question:

What if the system could stay in one numerical representation for more of the operation?

The prototype went by “Edge Glider” for months. The name TETRA came from an anonymous online chat: Mickey asked what to call it, and the answer was simply “Tetra.” It is the Greek word for four, and the tetrahedron is the simplest complex graph.

The distinction between an LLM and a database matters. LLMs use trained, probabilistic representations. TETRAbase uses exact numerical operations: it tokenizes a query, maps it to algebraic operations, and applies sparse and dense matrix operations and vector mathematics to stored data. The goal is not a plausible answer, but the exact result of a database query.

Mickey calls TETRAbase a matrix database. Every database needs a query language. So, how do you query a matrix database?

TETRAbase began by supporting openCypher, the graph query language associated with Neo4j, and later added SQL. Neo4j is the established reference point in the graph database market, making it a natural choice for both query language compatibility and performance comparisons.

Adding support for SQL was partly pragmatic: some organisations are more comfortable approaching their data through SQL than through a graph interface. But there is a deeper architectural point.

If the data itself is represented in a matrix, the query language is an interface to that representation. As Mickey put it: “If the matrix is the data, I can wire up any query language against this matrix.”

That is different from translating graph queries into joins over a relational database. In TETRAbase, SQL and graph queries operate on the same matrix representation.

TETRA calls the design Collapsive Architecture: structure, storage and execution are brought together in one linear-algebra space rather than maintained as separate layers.

Linear algebra in graph engines is not new. FalkorDB, for example, documents the use of sparse adjacency matrices and matrix operations. The distinction Mickey draws is that TETRA carries the matrix approach through the data model and storage layer as well as query execution, storing the matrix in tiles on disk and assembling what each query needs.

In his origin story, Mickey describes the Data Matrix as recursive: relationships between entities can themselves be represented as matrices, keeping entities and their connections within the same underlying structure.

TETRAbase does not keep the entire data set in RAM. Rather than keeping the entire database in RAM, TETRAbase loads only the portions of data needed to answer a query into working memory, releasing that memory as the query progresses. The footprint falls instead of remaining tied up holding the full graph.

The execution uses multicore CPU calculations; it does not require GPUs in the database layer. Mickey describes the contrast between continuous mathematical operations and the repeated pauses involved in fetching data and resuming the calculation vividly:

“The query goes through the processor like a wood chipper.”

The practical proposition is faster query execution, less memory held per query, a smaller storage footprint and fewer tuning parameters. TETRAbase runs with no indexes or cache and is encrypted on disk.

“TETRA’s all math, so there’s really no index”, as Mickey puts it.

According to TETRA’s benchmark report, TETRAbase is 66x faster than Neo4j and handles 10.3x more queries per second, while using 2.1x less memory, 13x less CPU and 7.9x less disk space and being encrypted on disk. The report presents the measurements, methodology and cases where the comparison is less favourable.

These are company-published results, not an independently audited certification. The point here is the architecture that enables a combination of fast results and lean operation, not a leaderboard against any one vendor.

But how does the architecture translate into business terms? Mickey’s answer was concrete: fewer machines, less operational effort and the potential to run workloads that once required a cluster on a single server.

Moving from three database servers to one is visible on a cloud bill. TETRAbase does not need indexes or caches; fewer tuning surfaces also mean fewer operational tasks, and risks.

TETRA is designed to run in the customer’s own cloud, close to the systems that use the data. Offering TETRAbase via a SaaS model is possible, but Mickey argues that an external SaaS call would add network latency and dilute performance gains. He described the licensing model as based on instance and graph size, rather than per-query charges.

There is a bigger context for this focus on efficiency. Data centres’ electricity demand, water use, land requirements and effects on local power prices have become public issues. In U.S. local elections on November 3, voters backed restrictions or rejected data-centre development proposals. The social licence for the AI infrastructure buildout cannot be taken for granted.

This is where TETRA’s status as a Public Benefit Corporation matters. The company’s stated mission includes building technology that uses fewer resources, emits less carbon and expands access to useful tools.

Mickey says TETRA’s internal modelling points to the possibility of reducing electricity consumption by more than 40% across the infrastructure used to store and query data. He is clear that this is a projection based on the company’s modelling, not a measured deployment result.

It will only be possible to validate this at scale, and it should not be read as a claim about the energy used by GPU compute for training or inference. That distinction matters.

Efficiency claims are easy to make and harder to prove across real workloads. But as AI systems multiply, the answer cannot always be to add more infrastructure. Better software and more efficient use of existing hardware belong in the conversation too.

For Mickey, the database is the first application of a more general idea. He invokes a line attributed to computer scientist Edsger Dijkstra: “Simplicity is prerequisite for reliability.” It is a succinct way to frame the ambition.

Much of today’s software architecture is assembled from specialised services, APIs, databases, orchestration layers, security controls and observability tools. Each may solve a legitimate problem. Together, they can create systems that are difficult to understand, operate and trust.

Mickey is careful about where technology can and cannot simplify things. Data has an irreducible dimension involving semantics, ontology and meaning: where information came from, what it represents and whether it should be trusted.

A faster database cannot answer those questions. But once data enters a system, he argues, there is scope to simplify how it is stored, processed, moved and acted upon.

That is the ambition behind TETRAplex, the next step on the roadmap.

Mickey describes this as a way to assemble business workflows, connect them to LLMs and control the context each step receives. Failures should be handled explicitly and every change should have an identifiable actor. The aim is to make workflows reliable and observable before adding more autonomy.

Mickey made a point that is relevant to the current agentic AI conversation: “You can’t really have agentic workflows until you have reliable workflows.”

In his view, an API flow and an agentic workflow are not fundamentally separate species; the difference is the level of autonomy. That is why he sees data, APIs and AI as parts of one architecture, rather than components that should be bolted together as separate systems..

Today, TETRAbase is running on beta servers for initial design partners, prospective customers, as well as powering TETRA’s own applications. The core infrastructure has been stable for several months, with ongoing work to test edge cases and improve correctness.

One check is to run the same data and query through TETRAbase and Neo4j, using the established graph database as a correctness reference. The story is not that existing graph databases are invalid; TETRA is exploring a different way to build.

TETRA has also been working with independent collaborator HorneSci on the mathematical foundations and code correctness. That is distinct from the performance benchmark, which remains TETRA’s own report.

The immediate next step is to onboard more design partners, understand their problems and deploy TETRA where it can make a measurable difference.

The team will be at Connected Data London on November 11–12. For graph users, data architects and technology leaders, it is a chance to ask where a different data model might simplify existing workloads.

I started this journey  expecting to learn about another graph database. I came away thinking about a broader question: whether the way we represent, store and execute data is ready for a rethink.

TETRAbase is the first test of that proposition; TETRAplex is the larger ambition. Neither should be taken on faith. Both deserve to be examined through architecture, evidence and real deployments.

Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9668. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

For more fall baking inspiration, check out our Fall Flavor Edit.

#9667. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9666. Keeping bots out of a small forum without locking real people out: five layers and a checklist

People keep saying forums and private communities are coming back. As feeds fill up with generated filler, a quiet place with real people and a searchable history starts to look valuable again. Plenty of others disagree and say forums never really come back. Either way, the people running small forums have run into the same practical problem: once a place is worth visiting, it's worth spamming.

Across the communities we follow, the same situations come up again and again. An independent forum operator says plainly that they don't have the resources of the big social networks to fight slop and bot sign-ups. A site owner asks why bots register accounts on a WordPress site that has no public posting at all. A moderator describes "sleeper" accounts that sign up, sit quietly for weeks, then edit an old harmless post into a link farm. Several people warn about a popular forum plugin with a database injection flaw under active attack, and remind everyone that the fix only helps if someone actually installs the update. A person running a tiny forum says what keeps it alive is a calm weekly digest email, not growth hacks.

Put together, the picture is consistent. Small forums don't lose to one big attack. They lose to a steady drip of junk that wears out the one or two volunteers who moderate.

So here is how we think about defence, ordered by how much each layer costs real members. Start at the top and only move down when you need to.

Most bots are not clever. They hit every signup form they can find and see what sticks.

Many owners stop here and see the bulk of junk accounts disappear.

This is the layer that does the most work for the least friction.

Real newcomers rarely notice these limits. A genuine first question doesn't need three links and a signature.

This is where sleeper accounts get caught.

Some forums attract targeted abuse. Then you might need visible challenges at signup, invite-only registration for a while, or paid membership as a filter. These work, but they cost you newcomers. Use them as a temporary gate during a wave, then step back down.

Many "spam" problems are really security problems. An outdated forum plugin, theme or extension with a known flaw lets attackers skip all five layers and write straight into the database.

If you're choosing software, look at the moderation tools as closely as the features: approval queues, new-account limits, edit review and member reporting. Discourse, Flarum, phpBB, bbPress and the newer WordPress forum plugins all handle these differently. (Disclosure: we build Jetonomy, a forum and Q&A plugin for WordPress, so weigh our view with that in mind.)

The goal isn't zero spam. It's keeping spam cheap enough to handle that your moderators don't burn out, and keeping the forum open enough that a real person with a real question still gets in on the first try.

#9665. How I Built an iPhone App That Unlocks Screen Time With Exercise

Solo iOS and Flutter developer. I build small iPhone apps (sourdough planning, trading card scanning, pet records, Screen Time blockers) and write a

Solo iOS and Flutter developer. I build small iPhone apps (sourdough planning, trading card scanning, pet records, Screen Time blockers) and write a

Solo iOS and Flutter developer. I build small iPhone apps (sourdough planning, trading card scanning, pet records, Screen Time blockers) and write a

Pull to Refresh is my iPhone app that locks the apps you choose and unlocks them for exercise reps counted by the camera (App Store). This is the developer side: counting reps from Vision joint positions, what Apple's Screen Time API lets a third-party app do, and the bugs that taught me both. What the app does for its users is in the user-facing post.

VNDetectHumanBodyPoseRequest runs on every frame of a 1280×720 front-camera feed. I keep joints with a confidence of 0.3 or more and drop the frame; nothing is recorded.

What kept the counter small: every exercise reduces a pose to one Double, oriented so that low means contracted and high means extended. Push-ups, squats and sit-ups use a joint angle, averaged over both sides of the body when both are visible. Pull-ups and jumping jacks use the nose's height against the wrists, divided by torso length, so standing further back doesn't change the number.

One state machine then scores all five; each exercise supplies two thresholds and a speed limit:

The gap between the thresholds is the hysteresis: the phase flips to .contracted below contracted, and a rep counts only on the way back above extended:

The raw value is smoothed first (smoothed + 0.35 * (raw - smoothed)), because joints jitter between frames. A third line, 35% of the way down, catches half-reps: dip past it and come back without reaching depth, and you get a hint to go deeper instead of silence. Up to eight frames of missing joints pass before the screen says it can't see you.

The tests drive the counter with synthetic geometry: a pose builder that produces an exact elbow angle, swept through a cosine at 30 fps. Ten clean push-ups must give 10, half-reps 0 and a hint, and twenty 0.2-second cycles, someone shaking the phone, at most 4. Not zero: smoothing and the speed floor limit how fast reps pay, but nothing recognises shaking as such.

One dead end. I saw zero reps on a screenshot from the start of a squat set, decided a knee angle can't be read head-on and moved squats to a side view. Later frames of that set were counting fine. I reverted it the same day and fixed the setup hint instead, which had been asking people to stand side-on in front of the selfie camera. Now every exercise opens on the front camera, so the person doing the reps can see the count.

Screen Time work is split across processes that can't call each other. The app picks apps with FamilyActivityPicker and gets opaque tokens, never names. A DeviceActivityMonitor extension wakes when an interval starts or ends or a usage threshold is crossed. Two shield extensions draw the lock screen and handle its buttons. A DeviceActivityReport extension is the only process that sees per-app usage, and it can only render a SwiftUI view: the app shows a "minutes left" card without ever learning the numbers.

They share state through App Group UserDefaults, plus a Darwin notification to tell a running app something changed. Each rule has its own named ManagedSettingsStore, so rules shield and lift independently. The monitor is handed nothing but an activity name, so the name carries the context:

Two documented limits shape everything: an app and its extensions can monitor twenty activities, and an interval can't be shorter than fifteen minutes. Schedules repeat daily, not hourly, so "five minutes an hour" costs one registration per hour of its window. Windows are capped at 16 hours, and one slot always stays free for unlocks.

Up to 1.4 the code did the obvious thing: intervalDidStart lifts the shield, the threshold puts it back. The docs for startMonitoring say callbacks may arrive as soon as you call it if the interval is running. Saving a rule re-registered every budget, the registration echoed intervalDidStart, and the shield came down. And unless an event opts into counting past activity, which needs iOS 17.4, it counts usage only from the moment it's registered, so a save handed a spent allowance back in full. Stopping an activity echoes intervalDidEnd, so switching a schedule off mid-lock shielded the rule I'd just been told was off.

The fix was to let no callback decide. Each one hands the rule, as it is now, to one apply, which asks a pure policy function whether it should be open:

That works because of a record: when a threshold fires, the monitor writes down that the allowance is spent for the current day or hour, so an echo finds the rule spent and keeps it shut. A save now registers only the rule saved, and only when something iOS enforces changed. From iOS 17.4, budgets pass includesPastActivity: true and count the whole day or hour however late they're registered.

Earned time is a one-shot activity whose event threshold is the time bought. The threshold counts use of those apps, so putting the phone down doesn't burn paid minutes. The interval end is a backstop: four times the unlock, between 30 minutes and 22 hours. It's registered before anything is stored or lifted; 1.4 did it the other way round, so a refusal at the twenty-activity limit left the rule open with nothing to close it. And unlock records once lived in one array that three processes read and wrote whole, so one could resurrect an unlock another had just ended. Each record has its own key now.

The shield's button belongs to the shield action extension, and for years it couldn't launch its containing app. The only way back was a local notification, easy to miss with a Focus on. My first version posted it and returned .close in the same breath; closing the shield lets iOS terminate the extension, and the notification sometimes went with it.

iOS 26.5 added ShieldActionResponse.openParentalControlsApp. Both paths:

#9664. Should every directory listing and job post expire by default?

Anyone who has run a directory or a job board for a while knows the moment. You open an old category page and half of it is out of date. A tool that shut down. A business that moved. A job that was filled long ago, or was never really open.

Across the communities we follow, this keeps coming up from very different angles. Directory owners who went back and link-checked their own listings found a big share of them failing. One found that a large chunk of the entries an AI assistant had added for them were dead within a year. Another noticed that "failed" wasn't one thing: some sites were genuinely gone, while others were just blocking automated checkers and worked fine in a browser. On the hiring side, people tracking job posts keep pointing at "ghost jobs": roles that stay up for months with no intention of filling them. When a big job platform pulled a large batch of fake postings, the discussion quickly turned to why listings were allowed to sit there in the first place. People starting niche job boards ask a related question from the other end: how do you make sure employers who post actually get applicants, so they come back?

And not everyone wants things to expire. One launch-site builder made "launches don't expire" a selling point, arguing that a permanent page keeps sending visitors long after launch day.

So here's the question: should listings expire by default?

We build directories and job boards for a living, and where we've landed is somewhere in between. Job posts should expire by default, with a short, clear window and an easy one-click repost for employers who are still hiring. For directory listings, we prefer a visible "last confirmed" date over hard deletion. Run a regular link check that treats "blocked" differently from "gone", send owners a re-confirm request, and move unconfirmed entries out of the main listings after a grace period instead of deleting them. Claimed listings with an active owner get the benefit of the doubt. Unclaimed, bulk-added ones don't.

None of this is complicated technically. The hard part is deciding the policy, writing it down where listers can see it, and actually running the check.

#9663. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

#9662. TypeScript Branded Types: Type-Safe IDs in Lambda

Posted on Nov 17 • Originally published at sascha-ms.de

TypeScript branded types give a plain string an invisible brand, so the compiler no longer mixes up a member ID with a book ID. Sounds like a detail. Yet exactly this kind of detail slips through every code review: two parameters of type string, passed in the wrong order once, and a record ends up under the wrong key in DynamoDB. No test fails, because the data looks perfectly valid.

I care about this topic because serverless backends are full of such IDs. Every Lambda function receives identifiers from an event, builds keys from them, calls other services and returns identifiers again. In this article I show you how a few lines of type code get rid of a whole class of bugs without executing a single extra byte at runtime. At the end you will have a small, runnable loan API for a library, built with the Serverless Framework.

Branded types attach a brand to a simple type such as string or number that only the compiler can see. This lets TypeScript tell apart two IDs or amounts that look identical at runtime. The biggest pitfall is an “as” on every corner: the brand belongs in exactly one place, behind a check at the system boundary.

Picture a small library app. Members borrow books, and every loan has a due date and a late fee per day. A typical function for this looks like this:

The call compiles without complaint. Both parameters are strings, so TypeScript is happy. At runtime this produces a DynamoDB item with the partition key MEMBER#B-123456. Nobody notices until someone wonders why a member is called “B-123456”. With money it gets even worse: you cannot tell from the number 50 whether it means 50 cents or 50 euros.

This is exactly where TypeScript branded types come in. They turn the general string into a specific MemberId type that behaves exactly like a string at runtime but is no longer interchangeable with a BookId for the compiler.

To see why the trick is needed, let’s take a quick look under the hood. TypeScript checks types structurally: two types are compatible if they have the same properties. The name of the type does not matter. Java and C# work differently, where the declared name counts (nominal typing).

For objects this is usually handy. For simple aliases, however, it means that type MemberId = string is just a second name for string. The alias documents your intent but protects you from nothing. By the way, the TypeScript team has known about the wish for nominal types for years: the issue “Support some non-structural (nominal) type matching” has been open since 2014.

Without a brand, MemberId and BookId are just names for string; with a brand, the compiler can tell them apart.

The solution is therefore a small trick. You add a property to the type that does not exist at runtime. Structurally, MemberId and BookId now differ by exactly this property, and the compiler can tell them apart.

The most common variant is an intersection type made of the base type and an object carrying a brand. A unique symbol serves as the key. TypeScript treats this symbol type as unique: two such symbols are never compatible with each other, and they are only allowed on const declarations or readonly static properties.

The declare matters. It tells the compiler “this symbol exists” without anything showing up in the generated JavaScript. After compilation a MemberId is a perfectly normal string again. And because the symbol is not exported, no other module can rebuild the brand by hand.

You will also find the simpler variant string & { __brand: "MemberId" } online. It works in a similar way but has two drawbacks: the __brand property appears in autocompletion, and any library that happens to use the same convention creates compatible brands. With the symbol you are on the safe side.

You only get a brand through a type assertion with as. If you did that all over the code, nothing would be gained. That is why the as belongs in a single function that first checks whether the value really fits. Such functions are called smart constructors: they are the only official way from a raw string to a branded ID.

The benefit is twofold. First, a MemberId can only come into existence in the rest of the code after it has been checked. Second, the format rule lives in exactly one place instead of being scattered across handlers, tests and helpers.

Now it gets practical. We build an HTTP API with a POST /loans endpoint that stores a loan in DynamoDB. Members have IDs like M-000042, books B-123456, and late fees are calculated in cents.

The tsconfig.json is deliberately short. What matters is strict; without strict mode, branded types lose much of their effect. Also add "type": "module" to your package.json, plus the scripts "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit" and "test": "vitest run".

Create the file src/brand.ts from above without changes. The three ID types build on it, each with a smart constructor. For new loans we generate the ID ourselves. The random generator can be passed in from outside so that the function stays testable.

Numbers work the same way. If you store amounts as decimal euros, you invite rounding errors. A Cents brand forces you to keep amounts as whole numbers, and the constructor rejects everything else.

Watch out for addCents: if you add two Cents values with +, TypeScript sees the result as a plain number again. The brand does not survive arithmetic. That is why the result goes through cents() once more.

In single-table design, keys are often composed of a prefix and an ID. A brand helps here too: a function that expects a PartitionKey will not accept some randomly concatenated string.

Now comes the crucial part. Everything that comes in from outside is unknown at first. At this boundary you check the data thoroughly once, and from then on the rest of the code only works with branded types. Zod is a good fit: first regex() checks the format, then transform() turns the string into the branded ID via the smart constructor.

🎬 Flow: where the brand is assigned – this animated diagram only runs on my site: watch it on sascha-ms.de

The service only knows branded types. It knows nothing about HTTP or JSON, which makes it easy to test. The repository is an interface, so the test gets by without AWS.

The DynamoDB repository uses the key functions from step 4. The condition attribute_not_exists(sk) prevents the same book from being stored twice for the same member.

The handler stays lean: read JSON, validate with Zod, call the service. It answers invalid input with status 400 without revealing internal details.

With branded types you want to check two things. First, the runtime behavior of the smart constructors and the handler, which Vitest takes care of. Second, the types themselves: wrong code should not compile at all. // @ts-expect-error is ideal for this. If the following line does not produce a type error, tsc reports an error because the directive is unused. This turns every such line into a small test.

Both checks run locally without AWS access:

Expected result: tsc finishes without output, and Vitest reports Test Files 2 passed and Tests 6 passed. If you delete one of the @ts-expect-error lines as an experiment, you will see the error message that protects you from swapped values in real code.

The serverless.yml creates the function, an HTTP API and the table. The Serverless Framework v4 builds TypeScript handlers itself with esbuild, so you do not need an extra plugin. Its IAM role may only run PutItem on exactly this table.

The response is a JSON object with loanId, dueDate and lateFeePerDay: 50. If you send the IDs swapped, you get status 400. To clean up, run serverless remove --stage dev.

A word on cost and security: the brands themselves cost nothing at runtime, because they disappear completely during compilation. The table uses on-demand billing, so a few test calls cost a fraction of a cent. Keep in mind that branded types do not replace input validation. They only document that validation happened. The actual security comes from the validation in step 5 and the narrowly scoped IAM role.

The most common mistake is as everywhere. If you write value as MemberId in every other place, you have brands but no guarantee anymore. A simple rule helps: as to a branded type only appears in smart constructors and test data. A lint check or a quick grep during review finds the outliers.

Second, the brand is lost at every boundary where data is serialized. Whatever comes from JSON.parse, DynamoDB, SQS or an environment variable is a plain string again. That is not a bug but intended: this is exactly where the next check belongs. When you read data from DynamoDB, a schema pays off there as well.

Third, brands do not survive arithmetic or string methods. memberId.trim() returns a plain string, cents(a) + cents(b) a plain number. Plan for these spots deliberately, as with addCents.

Fourth, you should not brand everything. A brand pays off where values are easily confused: IDs of different entities, units such as cents and euros or milliseconds and seconds, validated versus unvalidated values. For a display name or a description it adds little.

Fifth, and this one is easy to miss: brands from different sources do not match. An ID created with Zod’s .brand<"MemberId">() is not a MemberId from your own Brand type, even though both have the same name. The type check in step 7 shows this with the last @ts-expect-error line.

Zod ships its own solution with .brand(). The type returned by z.infer is then the base type plus a Zod brand. According to the Zod documentation, only the output type is branded by default, and since Zod 4.2 a second type parameter lets you brand the input as well. For projects where every piece of data goes through a Zod schema anyway, this is convenient.

Still, I prefer my own Brand type with smart constructors. The reason: the domain logic does not depend on the validation library. Service and repository only import ids.ts, and if you later swap Zod for Valibot or the Powertools Parser, only the schema file changes. Pick one variant per project, though, or you will trip over the fifth mistake from the previous section.

For me, TypeScript branded types are among the tools with the best ratio of effort to benefit. Five lines of type code, a few smart constructors, and a whole category of bugs shows up while you type instead of in production. Especially in serverless applications, where many small functions pass IDs to each other, this pays off quickly.

I also see the limits. Branded types are a convention, not a language feature. Anyone on the team who does not understand why they exist will cast them away at the first error message. That is why I would not introduce them as a big refactoring. I would start where it has already hurt once: with the two IDs that most often appear next to each other as parameters. And I would briefly explain to the team why validation happens at the system boundary and nowhere else.

Where I disagree: some articles recommend branding every single primitive value. That makes code hard to read and tests cumbersome. A handful of well-chosen brands achieves more than fifty that nobody can keep track of.

No. The brand exists only for the compiler and disappears completely during compilation. The only runtime cost comes from the checks in your smart constructors, and you need those anyway.

The terms are often used interchangeably. Strictly speaking, a branded type stays compatible with its base type, so you can read a MemberId anywhere a string is expected. An opaque type hides the base type completely. In TypeScript, the branded variant is the usual one.

Yes, because only the plain value is stored at runtime. When you read it back, though, you get a plain string or number again. That is why you validate data from JSON, DynamoDB or SQS again and reassign the brand there through the smart constructor.

No. The brand type from this article has no dependencies. Libraries like Zod offer their own brands, which is handy if everything goes through their schemas anyway.

Find a function in your code with two or more string parameters that expect IDs of different things. Create a brand type and a smart constructor for each of these IDs and run tsc. The error messages immediately show you where the values come from and where the system boundary really is. If you want to go deeper into validation, see how to validate Lambda events with Powertools Parser and Zod. For testing, Lambda unit tests with Vitest is a good companion, and you will find an example of validated uploads in the article on the S3 presigned URL.

Which two values get mixed up most often in your code? Let me know in the comments.

All code from this article, ready to run: smirowstanitzok/sascha-ms-examples

Tested on 11/14/2026 with TypeScript 7.0.2, Zod 4.6.7, Vitest 5.1.0 and Node.js 22: tsc --noEmit without errors, all six tests green. The serverless.yml was validated as YAML, not deployed.

#9661. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9660. Before You Renew Snowflake, Run These 6 Queries

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Snowflake renewals have an odd shape. The contract is negotiated by people who rarely open ACCOUNT_USAGE. The usage comes from people who rarely see the contract. Then, a few weeks before the term ends, finance asks data a simple question: how much should we commit to next year? And data finds out it doesn't have a crisp answer.

I sit between finance and data, so that question tends to land with me. These are the six queries I'd run before the call. Most need ACCOUNTADMIN, or a role that's been granted access to the SNOWFLAKE database. The two that read ORGANIZATION_USAGE need organization-level access.

Before anything else, split spend by service. Compute is usually the biggest line, but serverless features, storage, and data transfer add up, and they don't respond to the same fixes.

Without organization access, ACCOUNT_USAGE.METERING_DAILY_HISTORY gives the same split in credits, grouped by service_type.

The annualized three-month column is the number I'd anchor on. A full year of history includes months when the workload was smaller, so the last quarter is a better guide to next year than the last twelve months. Watch the trend too: if credits are growing a few percent a month, a commitment sized to today's run rate runs out early.

Note the column is credits_billed, not credits_used. Cloud services are only billed when they exceed 10% of the day's warehouse usage, and credits_billed applies that adjustment. Plan on what you pay, not on what you use.

A warehouse bills while it's running, whether or not a query is. Snowflake now attributes warehouse compute to queries, which makes idle time measurable:

The usual culprit is a BI warehouse. Dashboards fire a query every few minutes, each one wakes the warehouse, and the warehouse stays up for its whole auto-suspend window after each query finishes. Check the settings:

An auto_suspend of 0 or null means the warehouse never suspends on its own. For BI and ad hoc warehouses, 60 seconds is a reasonable place to start. Every resume bills at least a minute, so going lower rarely helps, and a warehouse that suspends sooner loses its warm cache sooner, so measure before and after.

Two habits make this query far more useful. Set a query tag in every scheduled job and BI connection (alter session set query_tag = 'dashboard:exec-weekly'), so cost groups by purpose instead of by service account. And look for the same query running over and over: group by query_parameterized_hash and sort by credits. A dashboard that refreshes every 15 minutes for an audience that opens it on Mondays is a very common find.

The classic hit is a staging table that's truncated and reloaded every day. Each load leaves the old data behind in Time Travel, and then in Fail-safe for another seven days. Make tables like that transient, which drops Fail-safe, and shorten their DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS. Dropped tables show up here too, still billing until Fail-safe runs out.

remaining_now and days_left tell you whether you'll run out before the term ends. on_demand_now tells you whether you already have: a non-zero on-demand balance means usage above your capacity is being billed at on-demand prices. This view can lag by up to 72 hours, and it isn't available to customers who buy through a reseller.

If you're on track to finish the term with capacity left over, ask about rollover before you sign. Snowflake's own billing data has a rollover balance source for exactly this case: unused capacity carried into a renewed commitment. Whether you get it, and on what terms, is part of the negotiation.

Your account team will bring its own projection. Bring yours, with the queries behind it. A forecast you can rerun in front of someone is hard to argue with.

Fresha runs a public MCP server behind its ChatGPT and Claude apps, launched 4 Aug 2026, but that server lets clients search salons and book, and Fresha has no merchant API. Checked 24 Oct 2026. The route for your own agent into your calendar, clients, sales and reviews is Cotlet.dev, which adds 17 Fresha tools behind one MCP address.

Cotlet.dev exposes one MCP server at https://cotlet.dev/mcp/v1. Your AI agent connects to that address once and then sees the Fresha tools as ordinary MCP tools, with names, inputs and results it can chain together.

Cotlet.dev works on the business side of Fresha (partners.fresha.com), not in the app your clients book in. When your agent calls a Fresha tool, this happens:

Fresha has no webhooks that we found (checked 24 Oct 2026), so your agent pulls what it needs when you ask. Cotlet.dev needs no Data Connector add-on and works with whatever your Fresha plan shows in the browser, Independent or Team.

Your AI agent's client may ask for a config file instead of a form, and this block carries the same address:

Cotlet.dev acts as the signed-in Fresha user, so it sees what that user sees. The tool tests are built and run with the workspace owner, so that is the safest account to start with.

Fresha tools come in four areas, 17 in total.

Your AI agent reads without pausing, so listing appointments, looking up a client, pulling a sales summary or checking reviews returns straight away.

Cotlet.dev holds actions that reach other people or change money until you approve them in the Cotlet.dev console. In Fresha, booking a client, cancelling an appointment with a client notice and posting a public review reply are the clear cases. The agent can prepare the action, but nothing goes out until you press OK.

Your AI agent can chain several tools from a few plain requests. This illustration follows a manager on a quiet morning, with each request and what comes back.

Cotlet.dev tests all 17 Fresha tools every 12 h, and tests the bookings and replies clients would see every 24 h. Those tests book, move and cancel in a separate test salon, with a marked client, and clear it within an hour.

Cotlet.dev lists every Fresha tool, with setup notes and answers to common questions, on the Fresha API and MCP server page. Cotlet.dev also has a guide to connecting Fresha to ChatGPT and Claude where you can read the same setup written for a wider audience.

Cotlet.dev is independent and not affiliated with Fresha, so treat it as an unofficial layer that gives your own agent a way into the Fresha account you already run.

#9656. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.
