#9655. How I Build With AI Agents

Posted on Nov 17 • Originally published at davidmorais.com

I work at Dark Magic Studios, a small team that shipped gitmoire, a git client with built-in AI features. I own the build on Booker Blitz, my wrestling management sim, and I'm part of a new product, Hexboard, that we're keeping quiet for now. I use AI agents to write a lot of first drafts. I don't let them decide what lands. This is how that works: the products, the agent setup, and the review rules I won't give up.

Booker Blitz is a wrestling promotion management sim where you manage your roster and book your shows to get the best ratings. You can read more at bookerblitz.com. It's keyboard-centric, with switchable themes. You scout and train talent, give people a gimmick and a face or heel alignment, and book title divisions and brand splits. During a show you sit in Gorilla Position and make live calls while the simulation feed scrolls, which is the heart of the game. Wrestling schools graduate regen wrestlers into the roster. There's the DataStudio, the official editor, and you can bring in custom datapacks from existing games such as .db or .mdb files. It runs on Windows and Linux, and it is 100% playable on Steam Deck.

The stack is TypeScript, React, Electron and Tailwind, with n8n handling some of the automation around it, mostly for community and marketing purposes.

During playtesting I fixed bugs fast with an AI coding agent: reproduce the bug, let the agent draft a fix, read the diff, test it, push. The agent never pushes for me. If I can't explain why a change works, it doesn't go in. That loop kept testers unblocked while the game was being shaken out. Once people are paying, the same fixes move onto branches with pull requests, because speed is no longer the right tradeoff.

The next stage is getting the game through Steam and supporting it properly.

gitmoire is my desktop Git client with an Agentic Development Environment (ADE). It's a hard fork of angkorGit, which is MIT licensed, and it's built on Rust and libgit2. Our fork is closed source for now, I was exploring ways to monetize it, but have ultimately decided that it should be remain free, so I'll be open sourcing it soon.

Part of the reason it exists is simple. GitKraken took almost 40 seconds to open on my machine. That's me timing it by hand, not a benchmark, but I open a Git client constantly and that wait got old. The other reason is the loop I work in now: a ticket becomes an isolated worktree, an agent writes there, and I review the diff before anything lands. I wanted that loop inside the Git client.

You can connect a Linear workspace and see your assigned issues in the sidebar. Issues from your Git forge get the same treatment. From an issue I can create a worktree on its own branch in one click, with the agent prompt already filled in and editable. I can also start a worktree from a pull request, and gitmoire fetches the PR branch without touching my current checkout.

The newer piece is orchestration. On the Agents tab I describe a task, or point at a Linear issue. An orchestrator agent asks follow-up questions and draws a battle plan. I approve it, and gitmoire deploys one agent per task into its own worktree. I pick the provider and model for the planner, the feature developer and the reviewer in Settings. The model menu lists the real models from Codex, Cursor, OpenCode and Antigravity. Agents coordinate through gitmoire agent commands, and done, waiting or blocked updates show up as badges and toasts. Agents live on their own tab, opened from Home or with Alt+A.

The quieter features are the ones I touch every hour. Repositories sit in named groups. The diff viewer can ignore whitespace, jump between changes, search a diff or a conflict, and open the file so I can fix it in place. Markdown previews in the editor. I save commit messages I type over and over as quick commits, press Alt+P, and gitmoire stages everything and commits. Those can be global or per repo, and I can undo a bad pick. A rebase or merge picks back up once the conflicts are cleared.

Hocus is the multi-agent harness we use across Dark Magic Studios. You point it at a project and it scaffolds a 13-persona cast from your stack, then hires them, so you get agents with a defined job instead of one general assistant trying to do everything.

The roles include a planner, an orchestrator, a reviewer, a feature developer, a founder, and the rest of the crew around them. You write a persona once as a SOUL.md file: a role, a voice, and a body of instructions. Hocus compiles that into the formats used by Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Antigravity, Command Code and GitHub Copilot. hocus init sets the project up. hocus cast scans the repo for languages and frameworks, tailors each persona, and compiles files for the tools you use. An interactive command deck in the terminal lets you inspect personas, track plans, and talk to the cast.

Then run hocus init in a repo. The project lives at github.com/dark-magic-studios/hocus and will be getting a nice update soon to improve memory for your projects using hocus 🚀

The studio's outward-facing work, posts and announcement cards especially, goes through a crew of specialized AI agents. One keeps track of what is in flight. Others write briefs, check claims against the source material, design the cards, or dig into the code and the research.

The pipeline runs in the same order every time. Sources come first, then a brief, then copy, then design, and then it comes to me. Nothing ships without my OK: not a post, not a card, not a reply. I lock the copy and I make the product calls.

The canon check is the piece I'd recommend to anyone doing this. Agents love to make a product sound better than it is, so unsupported claims get cut, and posts may only cite locked changelogs. The crew also checks subreddit rules. One subreddit I'd otherwise post in bans game ads, so it gets skipped.

A Reddit post of mine got called AI slop. Being accurate is not the same as sounding human, and that post didn't sound human enough. I rewrote the copy plainer: fewer flourishes, shorter sentences, more like how I'd explain something to a friend. I used to ask only whether a post was accurate. Now I also ask whether it sounds like me, and if it doesn't, it goes back.

That's why the approval gate exists. An agent can check a claim against a changelog. It can't tell whether a post will make a community roll its eyes, and it has no reputation to lose if it does. I do. When I'm deep in a fix, posts sit in the queue. I've accepted that. A slower studio that sounds like a person beats a faster one that sounds like a content farm.

Agents draft fixes, first passes of copy, project scaffolds and working branches from tickets. I read every diff before it merges, and I run the change before I trust it. I lock the wording and choose the tradeoffs, including the ones I later regret.

If you're building something like this, start with the boring rules. They do more than any model upgrade.

None of this is clever. It's what a careful team does anyway, with the difference that some of the team now works fast and never gets tired. Speed is the easy part. Judgment is what you have to protect.

The AI-slop comment taught me the most. I had a process that checked whether a post was true, and I assumed that was enough. It wasn't. A post can be accurate and still read like it came off an assembly line, and people can tell. So the question changed from "is this accurate?" to "is this accurate, and does it sound like me?" If the answer to the second half is no, it goes back, however good the facts are.

The other lesson is about patience. The approval gate makes me slower. Posts wait while I'm in the middle of a fix, and some go out later than they could have. I've stopped treating that as a flaw. The queue is the cost of having someone with a name and a reputation sign off on everything.

Booker Blitz is heading into Early Access, and I'm staying on it. That means the Steam launch, the bug reports that come after it, and supporting the game properly once people have paid for it. That's also when the review rules get stricter: branches, pull requests, and no more shipping fixes straight to testers.

For the studio, the attention goes to gitmoire and Hocus. gitmoire is going open source, so anyone can use it, read it and send fixes. Hocus is getting an update to improve memory for your projects, so agents stop starting every session from zero. And there's Hexboard, which I can't say much about yet.

I'm looking for my next role. I want to build products, and the systems that let a small team ship them without losing the plot: the tooling, the review habits, and the agent setup that keeps speed from turning into mess. I like working close to the product, owning a build from first draft to release, and I care about the unglamorous parts, like the approval gates and the smaller diffs, as much as the features.

If that sounds useful, start at davidmorais.com, then look at bookerblitz.com, darkmagicstudios.com, and GitHub at github.com/dark-magic-studios. I'm happy to talk through any of it.

#9654. Modernizing ACH: Why the Workhorse Rail Needs a New Engine

The ACH Network is the most important payment system most consumers never think about. In 2025 it carried 35.2 billion payments worth $93 trillion, up almost 5% in volume and nearly 8% in value over 2024, according to Nacha. Payroll, mortgage payments, tax refunds, insurance claims and supplier invoices all ride on it.

Yet the rail's core design dates to the 1970s: fixed-width files, batch windows and settlement measured in hours or days. For Arun Kumar, an IT consultant and enterprise solution architect with 20 years in banking and payments, that contrast is the opportunity. "ACH is not going away; it is growing," he says. "The question for every bank is whether its ACH platform is an asset it can build on or a liability it keeps patching."

His recommendation is direct. Banks should stop treating ACH as a back-office utility and modernize it as a strategic, data-rich, real-time-ready rail.

Kumar sees four pressures converging on ACH operations at the same time.

Speed expectations. Same Day ACH reached 1.4 billion payments and $3.9 trillion in 2025, growing faster than the network overall. Meanwhile RTP and FedNow have taught corporate treasurers that money can move in seconds. ACH platforms built around a single nightly cycle cannot keep pace with multiple daily windows and intraday liquidity demands.

Fraud accountability. Nacha's new fraud monitoring rules took effect in two phases this year: March 20, 2026 for the largest participants and June 19, 2026 for everyone else, per the Nacha Operating Rules. Originators, third-party senders and receiving banks now need risk-based processes to detect payments that are unauthorized or induced under false pretenses, such as business email compromise and vendor impersonation.

Data richness. Fedwire's move to ISO 20022 in 2025 raised the bar for structured remittance data. Corporates now ask why their ACH payments still carry 80-character addenda while wires carry full, structured detail.

Legacy technology. Many ACH engines run on aging mainframe code, maintained by a shrinking pool of specialists, with fraud, sanctions and returns handled in disconnected systems.

Drawing on work across ISO 20022, SWIFT, ACH/NACHA, Fedwire, RTP and FedNow, Arun Kumar recommends a five-part blueprint.

"Modernization is not about chasing the newest rail," Kumar says. "It is about making every rail, ACH included, run on the same intelligent foundation."

ACH will keep growing because it is cheap, reliable and universal. Business-to-business ACH alone reached close to 8.1 billion payments in 2025, up nearly 10%. The banks that win this volume will be those whose platforms treat ACH as one channel in a unified, real-time-ready payments hub.

Kumar's advice to payments leaders is to start with a clear target architecture and a 12-to-18-month roadmap of measurable wins: faster returns handling, cleaner fraud signals, richer data for clients. "The rail is fifty years old," he says. "Your ACH platform does not have to be."

This story was distributed as a release by Sanya Kapoor under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging Program

#9652. Designing Feedback Systems for AI-Powered Training Simulators: Lessons From PraxisAI

An AI training simulator becomes genuinely useful when it can do more than simulate a realistic conversation. It needs to help learners understand what happened, identify the skills they demonstrated, connect their behaviour to specific competencies, and show them what they can improve next.

That was one of the central product challenges behind PraxisAI.

The platform allows trainee counsellors to practise conversations with AI clients and receive structured feedback on their performance. Instead of treating the session as simply a chatbot interaction, the product turns the conversation into an assessable training experience.

That changes the engineering question from:

Can AI turn that conversation into useful, evidence-based feedback?

The second problem is where much of the interesting product work begins.

An AI training simulator creates a controlled environment where someone can practise a specific skill through an interactive scenario.

The AI may take on the role of a client, customer, patient, interviewer, colleague, or another participant depending on the training objective.

A useful AI-powered training system needs a learning loop:

Scenario → Interaction → Analysis → Feedback → Practice → Progress

The conversation creates the practice environment.

The evaluation layer explains what happened.

The feedback layer tells the learner what to do with that information.

And progress tracking helps determine whether the learner is actually improving.

That distinction is important when designing an AI training simulator as a real product rather than simply adding an AI chatbot to an existing learning experience.

Imagine completing a training session and receiving:

Which part of the conversation influenced the score?

A score without context can become another piece of information that the learner looks at once and forgets.

A useful AI assessment system needs to answer a more important question:

That is why the feedback experience in PraxisAI focuses on observable behaviour and competency-level assessment rather than treating one overall number as the complete answer.

A conversation contains a large amount of information.

For an AI training simulator, however, not every part of a transcript is equally important.

The system needs to identify the parts of an interaction that relate to the learning objectives.

Depending on the scenario, that could include:

This creates two useful layers of analysis.

This asks what those behaviours mean in the context of training.

Separating these layers helps prevent the evaluation from becoming a generic AI-generated summary.

One of the most important lessons when building an AI-powered assessment system is that the product needs to define what "good" actually means.

PraxisAI uses defined counselling frameworks and competency rubrics to structure the assessment. It supports different counselling approaches, including CBT, DBT, ACT, REBT, CPT, MBCT and SFBT.

This means the assessment can follow a structured chain:

Selected approach → competencies → conversation evidence → evaluation → feedback

The evaluation framework isn't an extra feature added after the chatbot.

A score becomes much more useful when the learner can understand what caused it.

"You moved into another question immediately after the client disclosed feeling isolated, which left less space to explore the underlying emotion."

The second version gives the learner something concrete to work with.

Behaviour → Context → Competency → Improvement

This is one of the most important principles when designing an AI feedback system.

The system shouldn't simply tell someone whether their performance was good or bad.

It should help them understand the relationship between their behaviour and the outcome.

Generic feedback is one of the easiest problems to create with generative AI.

Ask a model to review almost any conversation and it can produce familiar statements:

None of these statements are necessarily wrong.

The problem is that they could apply to almost anyone.

Useful feedback needs to be grounded in the actual interaction.

Observation: The trainee asked another question immediately after a client disclosed an emotional concern.

Interpretation: The conversation moved toward information gathering before the emotional response was explored.

Relevant competency: Reflective listening.

Possible improvement: Acknowledge and reflect the emotion before continuing with another question.

That turns generic advice into something the learner can actually practise.

A good AI feedback system should not only identify an action.

It should explain why the action matters.

This is particularly important in skills-based training because learners are developing judgement, not simply memorising rules.

"Several questions followed one another without giving the client much space to expand on the previous response."

The second explanation provides a mental model.

The learner can take that principle into the next session.

This is where AI-generated feedback can become more valuable than a simple scorecard.

Training and assessment have different goals.

During practice, feedback can help someone improve while they are learning.

During assessment, too much intervention can influence the result being measured.

That is why an AI training simulator can benefit from separating these experiences.

PraxisAI provides Practice and Assessment modes. Practice can support learning and coaching, while Assessment provides a cleaner environment for measuring performance.

This leads to a broader product principle:

Don't assume the same AI interaction model should be used at every stage of learning.

The underlying technology may be similar, but the user experience and evaluation rules should reflect the learner's objective.

Another challenge is that skills are rarely universal.

In counselling, for example, different approaches emphasise different techniques and competencies.

An assessment system therefore needs to understand the framework being practised.

The system may need to distinguish between concepts such as:

This makes the evaluation framework an important part of the product architecture.

The AI isn't simply evaluating a conversation.

It is evaluating the conversation against a defined model of competence.

One of the most useful principles for an AI evaluation system is knowing when not to make a judgement.

Suppose a competency never appears clearly in a conversation.

Forcing the system to produce a score creates false precision.

A more responsible approach is to acknowledge that there isn't enough evidence.

PraxisAI's rubric-based assessment can identify cases where there isn't sufficient evidence to evaluate a competency rather than forcing an unsupported conclusion.

This principle applies far beyond training systems.

Uncertainty is often better than a confident answer without evidence.

A reliable AI system needs to know not only how to produce an answer, but also when the available information isn't sufficient.

A single feedback report tells a learner how they performed once.

Multiple reports can tell them whether they're improving.

That changes the product from a collection of isolated AI sessions into a training system.

Practise → Review → Identify weakness → Practise again → Measure progress

Over time, the learner can identify patterns.

Perhaps overall performance is improving while one competency remains consistently weak.

Perhaps questioning improves while reflective listening remains inconsistent.

This makes future practice more targeted.

"What am I getting better at, and what still needs work?"

This is an important product-design question.

Some aspects of human interaction are difficult to evaluate reliably from text or structured conversation data.

This creates an important boundary for AI assessment.

A system should be explicit about what it can observe and what it cannot confidently evaluate.

For a conversation-based simulator, observable communication behaviour may be suitable for structured analysis.

Other dimensions may still require human supervision.

The goal isn't to make AI appear more capable than it is.

The goal is to make the parts it can evaluate useful and measurable.

From a product perspective, the complete system can be thought of as eight steps.

What situation gives them an opportunity to practise that skill?

Allow the learner to interact with the AI participant.

Analyse the interaction for relevant behaviours.

Connect observations to the appropriate evaluation framework.

Explain what happened and why it matters.

Give the learner a specific behaviour to practise.

This is the difference between building an AI simulation and building an AI training product.

One of the bigger lessons from PraxisAI is that the hardest part isn't necessarily making the AI talk.

The harder part is designing the system around the conversation.

These are product and engineering decisions.

AI can accelerate implementation, but it doesn't remove the need for those decisions.

That is consistent with how ThinkShift approaches AI-native product development: build something real, make the important technical and product decisions deliberately, and test the result against real use rather than stopping at a convincing demo.

Don't build the conversation first and figure out assessment later.

That decision influences the scenario, interaction design and data you need to capture.

If the system cannot explain why it reached an assessment, the learner may struggle to trust or use the result.

Not every competency will appear in every session.

The system should be allowed to say when there isn't enough evidence.

"Improve your communication" isn't a useful next step.

"Give the other person more space to expand before asking another question" is something a learner can practise.

A learner may need coaching while practising but a cleaner environment when being assessed.

The real value of repeated training comes from seeing whether behaviour changes over time.

PraxisAI also illustrates a broader lesson about AI product development.

The valuable part of an AI product isn't necessarily the model itself.

That is why building an AI product is different from simply integrating an AI API.

The product needs a reason to exist beyond the model.

For companies exploring AI product development in Dubai, the same principle applies.

"What user problem becomes meaningfully easier, faster or more measurable because of AI?"

The conversation simulation creates a repeatable practice environment.

The assessment layer makes performance measurable.

The feedback system makes the result actionable.

Progress tracking makes improvement visible.

The AI is important, but the product system around it is what makes the technology useful.

This is the broader approach behind ThinkShift's AI-native product development and validation work: build the smallest real product that can answer the important question, put it into use, and learn from what actually happens.

An AI training simulator is an interactive system that uses artificial intelligence to create realistic practice scenarios. It can simulate a conversation or situation, analyse the learner's responses and provide structured feedback against defined training objectives.

It can analyse observable behaviours in an interaction and compare them with predefined competencies or evaluation criteria. The system can then identify relevant evidence and generate feedback explaining what happened and what could be improved.

An AI feedback system uses artificial intelligence to analyse an interaction, identify relevant patterns or behaviours and provide feedback based on defined criteria. In training, it can connect observed behaviour to specific competencies and improvement areas.

Competency-based AI assessment evaluates performance against defined skills instead of relying only on an overall score. Each competency can have its own criteria and evidence requirements.

AI can evaluate some observable communication behaviours, particularly when they are represented in structured or textual interaction data. However, non-verbal communication, subtle emotional signals and complex interpersonal context may require human judgement.

Accuracy depends on the quality of the evaluation framework, scenario design, available evidence and AI system. AI assessment should therefore be grounded in defined criteria and appropriate evidence rather than treated as automatically correct.

Evidence allows learners and reviewers to understand why an assessment was produced. Instead of receiving only a score, the learner can see the interaction or behaviour that influenced the evaluation.

AI can support training and provide additional feedback, but it should not automatically replace educators, supervisors or professional judgement. Some aspects of performance cannot be reliably assessed by AI alone.

AI training simulators may have difficulty interpreting subtle emotions, body language, cultural context and other aspects of real-world interaction. They should therefore be designed around clearly defined evaluation boundaries.

The most valuable part of an AI training simulator may not be the conversation itself.

It may be what happens after the conversation ends.

A useful system should help answer four questions:

That is the thinking behind the feedback and assessment experience in PraxisAI.

The goal isn't to produce another AI-generated score.

The goal is to turn every practice session into a more useful learning opportunity.

Simulation creates the practice. Evidence creates understanding. Feedback creates the next step. Progress creates a better training loop.

#9650. When Your Crypto Turns Red: How to Respond to a Market Crash

You go into crypto expecting a return, preferably a steady one that doesn't take forever to arrive. Then prices fall, and the investment you hoped would reward you starts losing value instead. It's an uncomfortable part of investing, but it needn't become a personal crisis: anyone intending to stick around for years has to learn to cope with losses as well as enjoy the gains.

Experience and a carefully drawn plan don't guarantee a profit. In a market prone to abrupt price swings, with the fear and greed index reflecting changing sentiment, setbacks deserve a place in your thinking. A guide on how to buy XRP explains the practical steps of getting started, but learning how to handle a position that's losing value usually involves experience of your own.

Fortunately, you can do some preparation before a crash arrives. If you know which parts of the situation to examine and what decisions you'll need to make, you have a better chance of working through the difficulty with a clear idea of what you're doing. The following steps are a place to start.

Managing the feelings around an investment comes before managing the investment itself. Crypto's hectic price movements make that a demanding exercise, particularly in a downturn, when mounting pressure makes an impulsive response seem attractive. Keeping a clear head at that point takes effort; knowing in advance that you'll be tested helps you recognize what's happening.

A loss on screen isn't an instruction to panic. Whether you're thinking of selling or treating the fall as a chance to add to your holdings, the decision needs reasons you can examine. Otherwise, the fear pushing you out of a position and the excitement drawing you further in can both take over the process. How do you give reason a chance to catch up?

Start by stopping for a moment. That pause is a small achievement because it interrupts the rush to do something immediately, when the pressure can make it difficult to see beyond the next click. Once you've made room to think, use it to consider the situation before committing yourself.

If you've already worked out a strategy and know what you want from the investment, bring those goals back into view. Would the sale you're considering, or the extra purchase, actually help you get there? Spending a little time on that question can settle some of the uncertainty, because you're looking at the decision in relation to a purpose you chose before the pressure built up.

Once you've got a grip on your emotions, look at the downturn over a longer stretch of time. The damage to your investments can be frightening, and you may feel like getting out altogether. But consider how many declines crypto has already been through: rising and falling markets are recurring phases in its history, although some falls have lasted much longer and cut much deeper than others.

Volatility has been part of crypto for as long as investors have been putting money into it, so learning to live with rising and falling prices is one of the first lessons. The rollercoaster comparison fits for a reason. You can be enjoying a climb only to find yourself heading down again, with little certainty about where the next twist will take you.

Being in the red today doesn't tell you that recovery is out of the question. The wider crypto market has recovered from earlier falls, so its cycles offer some perspective when pessimism starts taking over. Keep the distinction clear, though: that history doesn't mean every project survives or that every coin returns to its old price.

One decline may look much like another on a chart while differing in what caused it, how severe it is and how long it lasts. Trouble inside crypto can be the trigger, from a failed project to the collapse of an exchange. Mt. Gox's bankruptcy in February 2014 is one such example: confidence in exchanges suffered, and the shock added pressure to prices across the market.

The pressure can come from wider economic events, too. In November 2021, the Federal Reserve chose to slow its asset purchases, so it was still adding to its holdings, but at a reduced pace. That's a change in monetary support, not the same thing as an exchange collapsing. Find out which influences have contributed to the decline in your coins: understanding the reason for the fall helps you judge what may follow and decide how to act.

Getting a crypto forecast right is difficult, and plenty turn out to be wrong. You can still read them for the different ways events might unfold, using the possible market directions to think through your options without treating any one scenario as settled.

Crypto's longer-term future isn't something you can pin down, but working through those scenarios should leave you better prepared to choose a course of action. If you think the lower price creates an opportunity, you could keep your coins or buy more to build the holding. If your assessment points to a more severe and prolonged fall, selling a weak asset may be the response you choose instead, accepting the loss if the sale is below what you paid. By then, you should be choosing a response to the situation, rather than making a trade just to silence the worry.

When you can't make sense of the outlook, you can choose to sell only part of the holding and keep the remainder in case prices recover. Whatever you decide, let your overall strategy and the amount of risk you can tolerate determine the choice.

#9649. Making 3D bowling run on a 2019 TV browser (Chromium 79, phones as controllers)

Friends are over, dinner's done, and someone says "let's play something." Half the room doesn't know the board game. Nobody has a console. But everybody has a phone, and there's a TV on the wall.

So I built yooo.games: you open the site in the TV's browser, everyone scans a QR code, and their phone becomes the controller. There's nothing to install, and you don't need an account. It now has 23 games. Some you talk and draw in (Find the Spy, Mafia with the screen as the host, Quick Pencil), and in others you swing the phone like a real object: a bowling ball, a revolver in a holster, a fishing rod.

How it works: open the site on a big screen, scan the QR code, play together

The games weren't the hard part. The TV was. This post is about that.

The reference device: an LG with Chromium 79

My test TV is an LG on webOS. Its browser is Chromium 79, from late 2019, on a weak ARM chip with a Mali GPU. So I set the build target to that device and kept it there:

The first versions of the 3D games stuttered and froze on it. The 2D games were worse. Here's what I found, in the order it hurt.

1. On this TV, Canvas 2D runs on the CPU and WebGL runs on the GPU

I measured every game on the TV. The three.js games (golf, bowling, curling) ran at 49-59 fps. The full-screen Canvas 2D games ran at 7-32 fps. The shooting gallery, a pretty simple game, managed 8 fps.

It's backwards from what you'd expect: the "simple" 2D games were the slow ones, because on this TV Canvas 2D is drawn by the CPU.

What fixed it: I stopped drawing with Canvas 2D every frame. Each sprite is drawn with Canvas 2D once into a "stamp", uploaded as a texture, and from then on a small WebGL layer only positions those textures. On a desktop the shooting gallery's frame went from 4.5 ms to 0.3 ms. On the TV it was still slow, though, for the reason in the next section. Six more games were moved over the same way.

There's a catch, and it took a while to learn: a stamp that gets redrawn costs a CPU paint plus a texture upload again. One game redrew its characters every 250 ms and their eyes every 120 ms, which came to 281 texture uploads in 15 seconds. Now anything that moves is a static stamp moved by a transform, and animations are a few pre-drawn frames, not redraws.

2. Many bufferSubData calls per frame stall the Mali tiler

After the move to WebGL, the shooting gallery still ran at 6-10 fps on the TV. JS timings, long tasks and even gl.finish() showed nothing wrong.

The cause: I rewrote one vertex buffer dozens of times per frame with bufferSubData. On a tiled GPU like Mali, the driver has to stop and copy the buffer when you overwrite data a pending draw still uses. None of that shows up in a JavaScript profiler.

What fixed it: I upload all vertices for the frame once with bufferData(..., STREAM_DRAW) and draw in pieces by offset. The shooting gallery went to 58 fps, with a 17 ms frame. Now there's a counter in every room's debug journal, "vertex uploads per frame", and 1-3 is normal.

![Shooting gallery on an LG TV: 8 fps with Canvas 2D, 6-10 fps with WebGL and many bufferSubData calls, 58 fps with one upload per frame]

3. Shaders compiled mid-round are a freeze

three.js compiles a shader the first time an object becomes visible. On a desktop you never notice. On the TV, the first bonus item in a round, the first new golf hole, or a laser sight that's hidden until you aim each caused a visible hitch, sometimes hundreds of milliseconds.

Things that quietly compiled new shaders:

The rule now: anything that can appear in a round is prepared at game start. That covers textures (initTexture), shaders (compiled against a warm-up scene), and pooled meshes that get hidden and reused instead of being disposed and recreated.

4. The DOM over the canvas was most of the main thread

Name tags over eight players, with only transform changing, took a fifth of the main thread: style recalc, layers, compositing. On the TV the overlay was relaid 100-170 times a second. Changing a font size every frame was worse. One game went from 19 to 54 fps and from 714 to ~0 ms/s of long tasks after I stopped doing that.

A sneaky one: the results screen with faces and medals was rebuilt on every state update (a spectator joined, someone sent an emoji reaction). On the TV each rebuild was a 1-3 second task with zero lines of JS in the profile, just the browser decoding and rasterizing every image again.

5. Chromium 79 doesn't know half of modern CSS

The bundler lowers syntax, but CSS is on you. Chromium 79 has no :has(), no gap in flexbox (my drawing albums sat glued together on the TV), no aspect-ratio, :is(), @container, dvh or color-mix(). CSS built in JS strings isn't touched by the minifier at all, and one :focus-visible in a selector list drops the whole rule, :hover included.

There's now a guard in the build report that scans everything shipped to the screen for features Chromium 79 doesn't have, and it fails the build.

Walking to the living room after every change doesn't scale to 23 games. So there's a tvcheck script: headless Chrome with Canvas 2D acceleration off, CPU throttled Г—20, the TV's exact window size, and the game playing itself with bots. It reports fps, frame p95, long tasks, and the same counters as the TV journal (draw calls, vertex and texture uploads per frame, new shaders, DOM rebuilds per second), each with the line of code that caused it.

Its numbers aren't the TV's numbers. Chrome doesn't slow down the GPU, and some TV hitches never show up on a desktop even with a software GPU. But anything that's expensive under Г—20 is expensive on the TV too. So I compare traces before and after a change rather than chasing fps.

And there's an even weaker tier. Some TVs in the wild have no WebGL 2, or run Chromium 38. Those get a "superlite" mode: only the games whose screen has no WebGL and draws only when something changes (quiz, spy, drawing games, Mafia). The rest are shown greyed out, with an honest "won't run on this TV".

Bowling reads devicemotion while you hold a button, and computes the throw the moment you let go.

!A throw in yooo.games bowling: the ball rolls down the lane, then a spare

None of it was tuned by eye. There are 58 recorded real throws from Android phones and iPhones as test fixtures. The physics (Rapier, 120 Hz) runs on the server with no renderer, and a sweep script throws thousands of balls across a grid of speeds and spins. The screens only replay 30 snapshots a second, about 150 ms behind, so a weak TV never runs the physics, and a second screen in the room shows the same game.

!Quick Pencil: three players drew "fish" on their phones, the TV shows all three drawings

You can try it on any TV, laptop or projector: yooo.games. Bowling works with one laptop and one phone. With friends, start with Find the Spy or Quick Pencil. I've only tested one TV model properly, so if you have a Samsung, an Android TV or anything else, I'd love to hear what breaks.

Part of the code, and the first draft of this post, were written with an AI assistant (Claude). The measurements, the TV and the living-room playtests are real.

#9648. What Narcissists, Psychopaths And Sadists Have In Common

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Narcissists, psychopaths, sadists and manipulative people share a dark personality core that predicts selfish and antisocial choices.

This common tendency helps explain whether people exploit others, retaliate against them or refuse to trust them.

The crucial feature is a willingness to pursue personal interests at other people’s expense, accompanied by beliefs that justify doing so.

Known as the dark factor of personality, or D, this tendency brings together traits that can look quite different on the surface.

Narcissism involves an inflated sense of self-importance, Machiavellianism centres on manipulation, psychopathy includes callousness, and sadism involves enjoying others’ suffering.

The idea that these traits share an underlying disposition was established in earlier research examining their overlap and links to harmful behaviour (Moshagen et al., 2018).

The latest findings suggest that this shared core is more consistently associated with antisocial decisions than any of the four traits considered separately.

In other words, knowing what these personalities have in common may reveal more about their choices than knowing which particular label fits them.

The research involved over 10,000 people across ten studies using eight types of decision-making game.

Participants completed personality questionnaires before making hypothetical choices involving another person they did not know.

Depending on the game, they could decide how much money to share, whether to return someone’s trust, whether to retaliate or whether to cooperate.

Some situations allowed people to benefit themselves at someone else’s expense, while others explored whether they would trust another person when cooperation could benefit both.

People scoring higher on the dark factor consistently made fewer prosocial choices across all eight games.

The individual dark traits also generally predicted less prosocial behaviour, but their associations were weaker.

Once their shared dark core was taken into account, the separate traits usually added little to the explanation.

There were a few exceptions, particularly involving Machiavellianism in situations where distrust could influence decisions.

One possible explanation is that dark personality traits combine harmful tendencies with other characteristics that are not inherently antisocial.

For example, boldness does not necessarily involve harming anyone, while wanting admiration does not automatically mean exploiting others.

Earlier research proposed that these additional characteristics help distinguish dark traits from one another, while their shared core captures what makes them socially harmful (Bader et al., 2023).

Measuring a broad trait such as psychopathy may therefore mix callous self-interest with features that have little relevance to a particular moral decision.

Focusing on the common core could provide a clearer picture of someone’s willingness to disregard other people’s welfare.

Importantly, the dark factor extends beyond wanting a larger share of the rewards.

It also encompasses a readiness to hurt others and beliefs that can make selfish conduct seem acceptable.

Distrust may fit this pattern because expecting other people to behave selfishly can provide a convenient justification for doing the same.

That is a proposed psychological explanation, rather than evidence that distrust caused the choices observed here.

The findings do not mean that everyone with dark traits will behave selfishly in every situation.

Nor do they establish that personality caused the decisions participants made.

All the games were hypothetical, so participants were describing what they would choose rather than making decisions with real financial consequences.

This matters because associations between dark traits and antisocial choices can be stronger in hypothetical situations than when money is genuinely at stake.

Participants also volunteered through a website offering dark-personality assessments, so they were not a representative sample of the wider population.

Even with these qualifications, the results support a simpler account of apparently different dark personalities: much of their connection to harmful choices lies in the same underlying disregard for others.

The study was published in the journal Judgment and Decision Making (Hilbig & Thielmann, 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9647. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”

#9646. Can We Build Human-Like AI Before We Understand the Human Condition?

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

The technology industry is racing to build artificial intelligence that can reason, communicate and increasingly behave in ways that seem human.

But there is an obvious paradox in that ambition: science still does not fully understand the extraordinary mind we are trying to reproduce.

In 2016, __an editorial in the academic journal *History of the Human Sciences *__presented the problem in stark terms: despite incredible advances in fields such as molecular biology, evolutionary psychology, artificial intelligence and cognitive neuroscience, one central category continued to resist definition: “the human.”

The importance of that problem had been expressed more directly decades earlier by psychologist B. F. Skinner, who wrote in his 1974 book About Behaviorism that that “the major problems facing the world today can be solved only if we improve our understanding of human behavior.”

That question has become even more relevant as AI systems have grown more capable. What exactly are the characteristics that distinguish human intelligence? How did consciousness emerge? And how did our remarkable cognitive abilities develop alongside insecurity, aggression, cooperation, creativity and psychological conflict?

These questions form part of the much older scientific and intellectual problem of understanding the human condition.

Nearly four centuries ago, philosopher and scientist René Descartes, while probing the nature of the thinking mind, described the intellectual predicament in striking terms:

“So serious are the doubts into which I have been thrown…that I can neither put them out of my mind nor see any way of resolving them. It feels as if I have fallen unexpectedly into a deep whirlpool…”.

Almost four centuries later, consciousness remains one of the most difficult pieces of the puzzle.

Philosopher David Chalmers, co-director of New York University’s Center for Mind, Brain and Consciousness, famously distinguished the relatively tractable problem of explaining cognitive functions with what he termed the “hard problem” of consciousness: explaining why information processing is accompanied by subjective experience.

But consciousness is not only a question of subjective experience. It also gave humans an extraordinary capacity to understand the relationship between events, anticipate outcomes and increasingly manage behaviour on the basis of that understanding.

There is also an evolutionary puzzle. If the ability to understand cause and effect and consciously adjust behaviour provides such an advantage, why did anything approaching full human consciousness emerge so rarely in evolutionary history?

These questions are approached from different directions by philosophy, neuroscience and evolutionary biology. Together they illustrate how much remains unresolved about the mind that AI increasingly seeks to emulate.

They also raise another question about the human condition: what psychological consequences followed when humans acquired this extraordinary capacity for conscious self-management?

Australian biologist Jeremy Griffith approaches the problem from an evolutionary direction. His explanation of the human condition asks what happened when a conscious, understanding-dependent intellect emerged within an organism already equipped with genetically acquired instincts.

Griffith places the emergence of consciousness, and this resulting conflict with instincts, at roughly two million years ago, linking it to the major development of the brain’s association cortex during human evolution.

Natural selection can provide a species with inherited instinctive orientations, while a conscious mind develops understanding by experimenting with cause and effect. Griffith proposes that as our distant hominin ancestors became sufficiently conscious to manage life through understanding, their experiments inevitably began departing from established instinctive orientations. The instincts inevitably resisted those departures, and that orientating ‘pressure’ amounted, in effect, to criticism of an emerging intellect that could not yet explain why its experiments were necessary.

Griffith argues that the insecurity that resulted from this seemingly unwarranted criticism produced defensive reactions of anger, egocentricity and alienation. His hypothesis therefore interprets these troubled characteristics primarily as psychological responses to the emergence of consciousness rather than simply manifestations of selfish or aggressive instinct-based instincts.

Stephen Hawking once observed that while physics and mathematics may tell us how the universe began, they are “not much use in predicting human behavior because there are far too many equations to solve.” It is precisely this seemingly impenetrable complexity that Griffith’s hypothesis accounts for, presenting a framework in which the full spectrum of human behaviour, including its many apparently contradictory aspects, can be made sense of. Its proponents argue that the more fully Griffith’s explanation is understood, the more persuasive it becomes, a view reflected in the growing number of favourable assessments it has received from scientists and academics who have examined his work.

This also gives the hypothesis a further implication. If the insecurity arose because the conscious intellect could not explain why it had to depart from instinct, Griffith argues that gaining that understanding would resolve the original conflict. On his account, anger, egocentricity and alienation are therefore not immutable features of human nature, but defensive responses that can become redundant once their underlying cause is understood.

To advance research, discussion and public understanding of the human condition Griffith established the international charity Fix The World.

Neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene, who’s based at the Collège de France, has approached consciousness from a very different direction. His global neuronal workspace model proposes that conscious access occurs when information becomes globally available across a distributed network of brain regions, allowing it to be shared with otherwise specialised cognitive systems.

Chalmers, Dehaene and Griffith are therefore asking different questions and proposing fundamentally different explanations. Chalmers focuses on why subjective experience exists, Griffith on the evolutionary and psychological consequences of consciousness emerging in humans, and Dehaene on the neural mechanisms associated with conscious access.

Together they illustrate a larger point: understanding consciousness remains a substantial scientific and philosophical frontier.

For AI developers, the immediate challenge is not necessarily to solve the human condition. Today’s systems can reproduce remarkable aspects of human language and reasoning without requiring science to possess a complete theory of human nature.

But the closer the ambition moves toward genuinely human-like intelligence, the more difficult the unanswered questions become to ignore.

What distinguishes intelligence from consciousness? How did human consciousness arise? Why are emotion, insecurity, morality, cooperation and conflict so deeply entangled with human cognition? And which of these characteristics, if any, would accompany a genuinely conscious artificial intelligence?

What there is instead is a continuing endeavour across neuroscience, evolutionary biology, psychology, philosophy and now artificial intelligence to understand the mind that makes us human.

#9645. Why thinking longer helps: test-time compute and the new scaling axis

Posted on Nov 17 • Originally published at Medium

In September 2024, OpenAI released a model that did something strange. Asked a hard question, it paused. It produced a long, hidden chain of thought, reconsidered its own steps, and only then answered. On competition math and coding problems it was dramatically better than the models before it, and the improvement did not come from a bigger model or more training data. It came from spending more computation at the moment of answering.

That release marked a shift in how the field thinks about scaling. For years, the recipe for a better model was fixed: train a bigger model on more data. Test-time compute adds a second axis. Instead of training harder, you let the model think longer. This post explains what that means mechanically, why it works, where it stops working, and why it changes the economics of building with language models.

Test-time compute is any computation spent per query, after training is finished. Training compute is spent once, up front, to produce the weights. Test-time compute is spent every time the model answers a question, and you decide how much to spend on each question.

The first is to sample many answers and pick the best one. Instead of generating a single response, the model generates ten, or a hundred, and you keep the answer that shows up most often. This is called self-consistency, and it works for a simple reason: on many problems, the model gets the right answer some of the time but not every time. If it is right 30 percent of the time on a single try, and the right answer is the most common one across many tries, then voting across samples turns a sometimes into a usually. The technique was introduced by Wang and colleagues in 2022, and it remains the simplest way to buy accuracy with compute.

The second way is to search. Instead of sampling complete answers independently, the model explores a tree of partial solutions, and a second model, called a verifier, scores each step and prunes the bad branches. This is the same idea as a chess engine searching through moves, except the moves are sentences and the evaluation function is learned. The verifier can be an outcome reward model, which scores only the final answer, or a process reward model, which scores each intermediate step. Process reward models are more expensive to train, because they need labels for steps rather than just for final answers, but they catch errors earlier, before a wrong step poisons the rest of the solution.

The third way is to revise. The model writes an answer, critiques it, and rewrites it, repeating the loop until the answer stops improving. This is sequential rather than parallel: one long chain of reasoning instead of many short ones. OpenAI's o1 and DeepSeek-R1 both use long chains of thought produced this way, trained with reinforcement learning that rewards correct final answers and lets the model discover behaviors like backtracking and self-correction on its own.

If you work on diffusion models, the third mechanism should feel familiar. A diffusion model also improves its output iteratively, starting from noise and refining step by step. The difference is the medium. A diffusion model refines a continuous representation across denoising steps, while an autoregressive model refines text across tokens. In both cases, the core idea is the same: the first attempt is a draft, and extra computation is spent turning the draft into something better.

There is a puzzle here. If the model already knows the answer, why does it not just give it the first time? And if it does not know the answer, how does generating more text help?

The answer is that a language model is a distribution over continuations, not a single answer. When you ask it a question, it assigns probabilities to many possible responses. Greedy decoding, the default, picks the most likely token at each step and produces the single most likely response. But the most likely response is not always the correct one. Sampling from the distribution instead produces a variety of responses, and on reasoning problems, the correct answer often appears among them even when it is not the top choice.

This is easiest to see with a concrete measure. Researchers distinguish pass@1, the chance the first sample is correct, from pass@k, the chance that at least one of k samples is correct. On hard math problems, pass@k can be far higher than pass@1. The gap between them is the headroom that test-time compute exploits. The knowledge is in the model; the problem is reaching it reliably. Sampling, voting, and search are different ways of reaching it.

But reaching it requires a way to tell the right answer from the wrong ones, and that is where the verifier comes in. For math and code, verification can be exact: run the code, check the final number. For open-ended questions, verification is itself a learned judgment, which brings us to the central weakness of the whole approach.

Every test-time method that goes beyond simple majority voting depends on a verifier, and the verifier is only as good as its training. This is the same problem RLHF has with its reward model, and the failure modes are similar. A verifier can be gamed. A model searching against a learned verifier will find outputs that score highly without being correct, because the search is optimizing the verifier's score, not correctness itself. The longer you search, the more the verifier's blind spots matter.

There is also a deeper asymmetry. Verification is supposed to be easier than generation: checking a proof is easier than finding one. That is true for math and code, where an answer can be checked mechanically. It is much less clear for writing, planning, or open-ended reasoning, where there is no ground truth to check against. On those tasks, the verifier is just another model making a judgment, and using one model's judgment to select another model's output can amplify shared biases rather than correct them.

This is why the gains from test-time compute are uneven. On tasks with verifiable answers, thinking longer reliably helps. On tasks where correctness is a matter of taste or judgment, the gains are smaller and harder to trust.

The most systematic answer comes from Snell and colleagues at UC Berkeley and Google DeepMind, who studied test-time compute scaling in 2024. Their setup was deliberately careful: they compared different ways of spending a fixed inference budget, measured in floating point operations, against simply training a bigger model with the same total compute.

First, how you spend the budget matters more than how much you spend. A strategy that allocates compute adaptively, choosing the method and the budget per question based on an estimate of that question's difficulty, was more than four times as efficient as naive best-of-N sampling. Easy questions got sequential revision, which worked best there. Harder questions got beam search against a process reward model, which worked best there. Spending the same budget on every question, easy or hard, wastes most of it.

Second, on easy and medium questions, a smaller model given extra test-time compute could outperform a model fourteen times larger. The small model already had a non-trivial chance of solving those questions, and extra compute was enough to close the gap. This is the result that made the field pay attention, because it suggests that inference compute can substitute for model size, at least sometimes.

Third, and just as important, the substitution has limits. On the hardest questions, where the small model's success rate was close to zero, extra test-time compute added almost nothing, and more pretraining was the better investment. The authors' conclusion was that the two kinds of compute are not one-to-one exchangeable. Test-time compute amplifies capability that is already in the model. It does not create capability that is not there.

That distinction matters for how you read the recent wave of reasoning models. When a model trained with reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards produces a long chain of thought and solves problems it previously could not, part of what happened is test-time compute, and part of it is training: the RL phase taught the model how to use its thinking time well. The two are complements, not substitutes.

Test-time compute is not free, and its costs are different in kind from training costs.

The first cost is latency. A model that thinks for two minutes before answering is unusable for interactive chat, no matter how good the answer is. The second cost is price. Inference compute is paid per query, so a method that uses a hundred samples costs roughly a hundred times as much per answer. A lab can afford to train a big model once; serving it a million times a day at a hundred times the cost is a different budget. Snell and colleagues made this precise: when a model will serve enormous volumes of queries relative to its training, extra pretraining pays for itself, and test-time compute stops being the cheaper option.

The third cost is subtler. Longer chains of thought can drift. A model that reasons for hundreds of tokens has hundreds of chances to make a wrong turn, and once it commits to a wrong approach, extra thinking can entrench the error rather than correct it. Researchers have documented cases where longer reasoning produces confident, elaborate, wrong answers, and where a model talks itself out of a correct first instinct. Thinking longer helps when the model can check its own work. When it cannot, thinking longer is just more opportunity to be wrong with confidence.

There is also an open question about what is really being scaled. Is a long chain of thought genuine reasoning, or is it a more thorough search over patterns the model memorized during training? This is the same question I raised about diffusion models in an earlier post, and it has no settled answer here either. The honest position is that test-time compute demonstrably improves accuracy on verifiable tasks, and that whether the underlying process deserves the name reasoning depends on what you mean by the word. The behavior is real either way.

Test-time compute matters because it changes who can compete. If a smaller model plus thinking time can match a much larger model, then the advantage of whoever can afford the biggest training run shrinks, and the advantage shifts to whoever builds the best verifiers, the best search strategies, and the best ways of deciding how much to think about each question. That is a different kind of engineering, and it is more accessible to smaller labs and to academic researchers.

It also changes the research agenda. The interesting problems are now about verification: how to build verifiers that are hard to game, how to get process-level supervision without expensive human labels, and how to know when to stop thinking. They are also about adaptivity: spending a lot of compute on the questions that need it and almost none on the ones that do not. And for those of us working on diffusion models, there is a natural connection. Diffusion models are already test-time computers: their entire generation process is iterative refinement, and the number of denoising steps is a test-time budget you can turn up or down. The question of how to spend that budget well, and how to verify intermediate states, is the same question the language modeling world is now asking about chains of thought.

The first decade of scaling was about training: bigger models, more data. The next one will be about both axes, and about the judgment to use each where it helps. Thinking longer is a powerful lever. Like every lever, it works best when you know what it can and cannot move.

#9642. Launching smartclean: A CLI to Clean Up Your Dev Machine

Developer machines fill up quietly. node_modules, build caches, package manager stores, old tool data, and forgotten Docker layers add up to tens of gigabytes. smartclean is a small CLI that finds that cruft and removes it safely.

The scan output groups by category so you can see where the space went. Most machines recover 5-20 GB on the first run.

The default is conservative. smartclean will not remove a directory unless it can confirm it is regenerable (lockfile present, cache directory, known build output). If you are unsure, --dry-run shows exactly what would be deleted.

I kept running out of disk on a laptop with a 256 GB SSD. Existing tools either required a GUI or deleted too aggressively. smartclean is the middle ground: fast, terminal-native, and safe.

Feedback welcome. If it deletes something it should not have, open an issue with the path and I will add a guard.

The hardest part was not the scanning; it was deciding what counts as safe. A directory with a lockfile next to it is safe. A directory without one is not, even if it looks like a cache. When in doubt, smartclean skips and tells you why.

The first version is intentionally small: scan, preview, clean. Future releases will add per-directory allowlists and a JSON output mode for scripting.

These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. 1. ChatGPT

ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Cons:

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

2. DALL-E

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Pros:

  • Generates high-resolution images
  • Can generate images from text prompts
  • It can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as generating images of a certain style or category

Cons:

Grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text. It has several features that make it useful for improving writing, including:

  • Overall, Grammarly is a useful tool for improving writing, it can help users identify and correct grammar and punctuation errors, and improve the clarity, concision, and readability of their text. #9640. Modus CTO Explains Why Static AI Skills Are Becoming a Bottleneck for Enterprise AI

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

AI agents may be processing hundreds of lines of instructions to complete tasks that require only a handful of details. According to Modus, median context-loading precision is below 1%, while even results at the 90th percentile remain below 10%. The finding highlights a growing challenge for enterprise AI: providing agents with relevant, up-to-date knowledge without overwhelming them with unnecessary information.

In a recent blog post, Tomer Mesika, Co-Founder and CTO of Modus, argues that static AI skills are contributing to this problem. While these instructions encode organizational workflows and technical knowledge, they also contain operational details that inevitably change. As companies deploy more agents, keeping these instructions accurate becomes increasingly difficult.

Mesika proposes moving toward dynamic skills, where information is assembled at runtime based on the task, the current state of the organization, and the user's permissions.

Static skills often combine two different things: instructions describing how work should be performed and operational facts needed to execute it. The first might include deployment procedures or incident response practices. The second includes database names, cloud account IDs, API endpoints, Slack channels, and feature flags.

The problem is that these facts change constantly. A database gets renamed, a team changes its communication channel, or an infrastructure resource is replaced. The skill remains unchanged unless someone remembers to update it.

Mesika compares this to using a printed map after the surrounding infrastructure has changed. The instructions may look reliable, but their underlying information is no longer accurate.

MCP addresses part of the challenge by allowing agents to retrieve live information from connected systems. However, freshness does not guarantee relevance. MCP is the communication mechanism; the missing piece is determining what information should travel through it for a particular task and user.

Mesika's proposed solution is to separate organizational processes from the facts required to execute them.

Instead of hard-coding an account ID or communication channel into a skill, organizations can use meaningful placeholders such as "Production AWS account ID" or "On-call channel." The underlying process remains stable, while the corresponding information is resolved when an agent needs it.

"Static skills are essentially caches without invalidation. They preserve a snapshot of what an agent needed to know when someone originally wrote them, even as the underlying organization changes," said Mesika. "The goal should be to keep the process durable while computing the facts an agent needs for each task, based on the latest available information and the user's permissions."

This approach allows agents to receive just-in-time skills containing only the operational details relevant to their immediate requests.

Making dynamic skills work requires more than rewriting instructions. Organizations need infrastructure capable of collecting, connecting, verifying, and continuously updating their operational knowledge.

Mesika outlines an approach that pulls information directly from authoritative sources, including cloud accounts, Slack, Git, databases, feature flags, and internal documentation. Rather than treating this information as disconnected text, the system maps entities and their relationships.

For example, an agent working on a payments service should be able to identify its production account, associated database, kill-switch flag, and on-call channel. Each fact also needs metadata covering its source, last verification, ownership, and access permissions.

This is the foundation of a Context Warehouse: a continuously maintained layer of enterprise knowledge that supplies AI systems with the information they need.

Modus is developing this architecture through its platform, using connectors to gather organizational context from existing enterprise tools. Its Context Warehouse organizes information into context items with source details, hierarchical relationships, and permissions inherited from the original systems.

When an agent connects through MCP, it communicates its intent rather than requesting a specific file. Modus selects and assembles the relevant information, filters it according to the user's permissions, and measures how much of the available context was actually needed.

Permissions are also checked with every read rather than relying on previously cached access information.

For enterprise leaders, the takeaway is that improving AI agents may require rethinking the infrastructure behind the instructions they receive. Building dynamic skills involves continuous synchronization, entity mapping, metadata management, and permission-aware retrieval. These capabilities go well beyond prompt engineering or creating more specialized instruction files.

As organizations move toward more autonomous AI systems, the challenge will be giving agents access to knowledge that reflects how the business operates today. Static skills can preserve how work should be done, but a Context Warehouse can provide what agents need to do it now.
