#9639. URL to PDF in n8n and Zapier without code

Posted on Nov 17 • Originally published at siftwright.com

A lot of "save this page as a PDF" work happens in automation tools, not in application code. An agency archives every landing page it launches. An operations team saves supplier terms each time a new vendor is added to a sheet. A finance team keeps a copy of each online invoice page. Nobody wants to stand up a headless browser for this, and nobody should have to write a Python service for it.

Both n8n and Zapier can do it with a generic HTTP step that calls a URL-to-PDF API, then a step that downloads the file and drops it somewhere useful. This guide shows both, using the Siftwright screenshot endpoint in PDF mode. You can import the n8n workflow as it stands. For Zapier it covers the one limit that trips people up, the 30-second step timeout.

If you only need a PDF of one page right now, you don't need any of this: the free website to PDF converter does single pages in the browser.

Everything below wraps a single request. You send a public URL, ask for pdf, and pick a page size:

The response is JSON. Each page you asked for comes back as one entry in results:

Don't paste the API key into the node. In n8n, create a credential of type Header Auth with:

Call the credential Siftwright API. The workflow below refers to it by that name. After import, open the Render PDF node and select your credential if n8n doesn't pick it up on its own.

Copy this, then in n8n use Workflows → Import from File (or paste it straight onto the canvas):

JSON body built with an expression. JSON.stringify({ url: $json.url, ... }) builds the body from each incoming item, so one HTTP node handles any number of pages. Building it with JSON.stringify instead of typing raw JSON with {{ }} inside it means a URL containing quotes or ampersands can't break the body.

Timeout of 300,000 ms. The endpoint waits for the browser to finish, up to about 280 seconds for heavy pages. Most single pages finish in seconds, but a timeout shorter than the API's own limit gives you a failed node while the render may still succeed on our side.

Batching: 1 item every 2 seconds. n8n sends all items in parallel by default. One at a time with a short gap keeps a 500-row sheet well under the 60-requests-per-minute limit, and it's easier on the sites you're capturing.

Retry on fail, 2 tries, 5 seconds apart. This covers the occasional network blip or 502. Don't raise it much: a 401 or 402 will fail every time, and you want to see that quickly.

A Code node instead of an IF node. The response nests the result inside an array, and the useful fields (the page's name, the error message) live in two different nodes. Six lines of JavaScript are clearer than an IF node plus an expression for every field. Failed pages show up in the execution log with their error message.

Download as a file. Setting the response format to File puts the PDF in the item's binary property data, which is what Google Drive's Upload file, S3's Upload, email nodes' attachments and the disk-write node all expect.

Delete Save PDF, add a Google Drive → Upload file node, set Input Data Field Name to data, and set the file name to an expression such as:

Dating the file name keeps a history when the same page is captured every week. If you need copies you can prove haven't been changed since, see archiving web pages for compliance, which adds hashes and trusted timestamps.

We ran the exact workflow above on n8n 1.123.97 (self-hosted, imported with n8n import:workflow and run with n8n execute) in two ways:

We did not run it against /v1/screenshot with a real paid key for this post, so the response above shows the documented shape with the file link shortened.

Zapier has no node for us, but Webhooks by Zapier can call any JSON API. Note that Webhooks by Zapier is a premium app, so it needs a paid Zapier plan. A typical Zap:

Step 4 relies on Zapier's file handling. When you map a URL into a file field, Zapier downloads it and passes the file on, so you don't need a separate download step. Because fileUrl is a signed public link, no extra authentication is needed.

Use Custom Request rather than the simpler POST action. The POST action sends form-style data by default, and you'd have to fight its payload settings to get a clean JSON body. Custom Request sends exactly what you type in Data.

We didn't run this Zap ourselves. It uses only the standard Custom Request, Filter and Upload File steps. If a field name differs in your account, map it from the sample data Zapier shows after you test step 2.

Zapier stops waiting for an HTTP request after about 30 seconds, and you can't raise that limit for Webhooks by Zapier. That shapes how you use any rendering API from a Zap:

A timed-out step shows as an error in Zap history. Don't just replay it in a tight loop. Check whether the page is unusually slow first.

If your team already lives in Zapier and the pages are ordinary marketing or document pages, the Zapier recipe is the shortest path. If you're capturing hundreds of pages on a schedule, or pages heavy enough to take more than half a minute, n8n gives you the control you need.

Import the workflow, point Pages at your own sheet, and run it with two or three URLs first. A Siftwright API plan starts at $29 a month, and pages that fail to render aren't billed. If something in either recipe doesn't work for you, tell us at support@siftwright.com.

#9638. What is piloncillo? This sweetener makes great cookies, pan dulce, and more: Use this traditional Mexican unrefined sugar for a dash of flavor and history.

This article is part of our feature celebrating Pan Dulce. Find all things pan dulce here.

Categorically, piloncillo is a “non-centrifugal” cane sugar, meaning it is an unrefined sugar product and a true natural brown sugar. It’s mostly consumed in Mexico and Latin America, but a similar product can be found in Asia, known as jaggery in India. Though often lumped together, these unrefined dark sugars are very different from brown sugars on the market today, which have been refined to a large degree — in some cases, they’re actually just white sugar with coloring or molasses added.

Making piloncillo, on the other hand, involves an artisanal process that’s hundreds of years old. To make it, pressed cane juice is boiled to evaporate the water and deeply caramelize the sugar. The cooked cane is then poured into molds (often made of wood) and left to dry and harden. Traditional piloncillo is conical in shape and can vary in size from small to large cones but is most commonly found in a medium size that weighs about 200 grams. In Guatemala and Colombia, it is called panela, where it is cooked to a lighter degree and typically formed into a brick, rather than cone, shape. Other forms of piloncillo can be granulated or liquid (which is more rare).

Minimally processed and boldly flavored, piloncillo was historically a prized and respected foodstuff. As an unrefined cane sugar, piloncillo provides more complex vitamins and minerals than refined sugars, which undergo processing and whitening methods that also strip nutrients from the whole food. And piloncillo is also great for baking, providing notes of burnt caramel and hints of smoke. Plus, its rich molasses qualities keep baked goods moist and fresh for longer.

Always look at the ingredient label when purchasing piloncillo and make sure it says 100% pure cane juice or cane sugar. It is becoming increasingly common to find imitation products marketed as jaggery or piloncillo that contain coloring and corn syrup. You can find good piloncillo at specialty grocery stores or online at retailers.

In Mexico and throughout Latin America, piloncillo is an important ingredient in many traditional dishes. (Some will even say it’s not the “real dish” if you substitute sugar in these recipes due to the deep flavors and richness that only piloncillo can provide.) This deep, dark unrefined sugar lends its characteristic flavor and texture to popular foods and beverages such as capirotada, tepache, coyotas, atole, café de olla, calabaza al horno, coricos, and hojarascas, to name a few!

I love adding piloncillo when I’m making champurrado. In this warm and thick chocolate beverage, the piloncillo is chopped or grated and dissolved in the pot with water or milk before adding the chocolate and masa. In this recipe, the piloncillo’s intense sweet and smoky flavors pair well with the chocolate and corn masa.

While there are many dishes and uses for piloncillo, it’s not a simple substitution for granulated white sugar in recipes, but you can use it the same as you would brown sugar with a 1:1 substitution by weight.  Depending on how hard the cone is, it can be crumbled or grated for easier measuring. If it is very hard, try cutting it in half with a sharp knife and then placing it between parchment paper or a towel and beating with a rolling pin.

Find puerquitos and many more Mexican sweets in our feature celebrating pan dulce.

#9637. Ten paid calls, zero parameters: a 402 example is part of the payment contract

Posted on Nov 17 • Originally published at minia2a.uk

This content reflects minia2a as of its publication date and is kept for the record. Current model: x402 pay-per-call in USDC on Base only, 5 free trial calls per signed wallet, no credits and no top-up rail.

Between 2026-11-16T22:37:26Z and 2026-11-17T15:33:30Z, one automated buyer agent attempted the same paid endpoint ten times. It paid ten times — $0.10 each, $1.00 in total — and was refused ten times. All ten charges were refunded in full and each refund is marked sent with its own on-chain hash.

The buyer's client was not broken in the usual sense. It paid correctly, in the right scheme, on the right chain. What it sent after paying was an empty request. Not a malformed one, not a wrong field name — no parameters at all. And the reason is visible, in one JSON object, in the 402 that our own platform served it.

Each cycle is the same four steps, forty seconds to a few minutes apart: challenge, payment, empty request, refusal. Ten times, for seventeen hours. That is not a retry storm — the gaps are irregular and long — it is an agent that never learned what to send, because nothing in the machine-readable surface told it.

Here is the input example that our 402 carried for that endpoint, verbatim:

Every key is a real parameter name that some version of this handler has accepted. Every value is a sentinel. A human reads that and thinks "oh, it needs a captcha site key". A machine reads the same object and, quite reasonably, concludes there is nothing here worth copying — because copying a sentinel into a live request is worse than sending nothing.

That is what the buyer's gateway did. It builds calls from the advertised example. The example contained no usable values, so the request it built contained no parameters. The handler received {}, found no sitekey, threw a caller error, and the platform refunded.

The asymmetry that makes this a contract problem, not a docs problem: there is no way, in this 402 surface, to mark a parameter as required. The bazaar input block is an example, not a schema with a required array. So "which fields must I send?" is answerable only by looking at which fields the example gives real values for. An all-sentinel example answers it with "none".

It also would not have helped if the client had guessed the field name. The handler accepts both sitekey and siteKey, and both url and websiteURL — those aliases exist precisely because callers guess. This request did not guess. It sent nothing to guess with.

In x402, settlement happens before the handler runs. That ordering is the point of the protocol — you pay for the work, you get the work — but it also means a caller's parameter mistake is not a free 400. It is a charge, an on-chain refund, and a delivery row that reads refused. Ten times over, that is:

The last item is the expensive one. A buyer agent that cannot complete a call does not file a bug report. It reroutes, or it stops.

We sampled 192 of our first-party endpoint ids this cycle and read the advertised input example out of each live 402. Those endpoint ids rotate over a ten-day catalog cycle, so this is a sample rather than a census, but the distribution is clear:

One out of 192 is a small defect rate and a very expensive single instance: it was the one endpoint a real paying buyer chose to hammer.

Already live, no binary change needed: the service description on the 402 now names the three fields and marks one of them required, and the handler's 400 response names all three plus their shapes. Both changes are in production. Neither one is visible to a client that builds requests from the queryParams example — which is exactly the client we had.

Queued behind a gateway build (not live): replacing the sentinel example with a real, working one — a public captcha test key with its demo page URL, verified against the handler before it ships. We do not describe queued work as done; until that build lands, a client that copies our example still gets a refusal and a refund, and we would rather write that down than let the post read as a fix.

Our own rule, restated: an input example is not decoration. It is the only machine-readable statement of "what to send" that a payment client has before it spends money. An example that cannot be copied is worse than no example, because it looks complete.

If you serve an x402 endpoint, read your 402 the way a buyer's agent does and look for sentinel values:

If your example cannot be run successfully against your own endpoint, you have two options: make it runnable, or remove the fields and say plainly in the description that the caller must supply them. What you should not do is ship a full-looking example whose every value is a placeholder. That combination is how a buyer pays ten times for an empty request.

#9636. How Sprig Replaced Postgres, ClickHouse & Redis…with 4-8x Better Latency

Monstrously Fast + Scalable NoSQL. Start Fast. Scale Fearlessly

Monstrously Fast + Scalable NoSQL. Start Fast. Scale Fearlessly

Monstrously Fast + Scalable NoSQL. Start Fast. Scale Fearlessly

With ScyllaDB, a small engineering team could focus on building their product instead of battling their databases

“Just use Postgres” is the logical path for a startup figuring out product-market fit. But Sprig – an AI-powered product research platform – hit that fit much sooner than expected. And the sheer scale of the resulting data (over 1.3T events and 75 B attributes from 15B visitors) maxed out Postgres much sooner than expected.

At Monster Scale Summit 2026, Brendan Cox (Senior Staff Engineer at Sprig) walked through the full journey: why their seemingly simple platform hit database limits so fast, the various approaches they tried, and how their small engineering team worked through these challenges.

At the surface, Sprig’s core product seems relatively straightforward. Customers install the Sprig SDK into their mobile apps or websites to track user actions and attributes. When a user’s behavior matches the set criteria, Sprig triggers a targeted in-product survey. Because these surveys collect so much feedback, Sprig then uses AI to process and report findings for product researchers.

Under the hood, a high-speed data engine is required to evaluate all this user behavior in real-time. “What we built actually has a lot in common with analytics, ad tech or recommendation systems,” explained Brendan. “That is, it’s a low-latency, and compute and data heavy, system that must make decisions up to thousands of times per second.”

For a small startup, Sprig manages an impressive volume of data. At any given time, the platform tracks 15 billion distinct visitors across multiple devices. To understand those visitors, the backend maintains 75 billion user attributes and 20 billion different event counters, having processed over 1.3 trillion events to date (as of February 2026).

Sprig’s backend systems process 20,000 – 40,000 events and attributes every second. For every one of those incoming events, the system must evaluate the complex trigger criteria and decide whether to display a survey within milliseconds.

In the beginning, Sprig followed the classic startup playbook: they built their initial system on PostgreSQL (they opted for the Amazon Aurora flavor). As Brendan noted, “This is exactly where every startup should start off. Basically, just do the simple thing and get product market fit”.

Sprig found that fit remarkably fast. However, as larger and larger customers came onto the system, they hit the limits of Postgres. Per Brendan, “We had high write throughput, which was saturating a single writer instance in Aurora. We also reached the maximum number of reader instances and maximum instance size available to us at the time in AWS. This was incredibly expensive for our company. It was absolutely imperative to get off this system as soon as possible and onto something new.”

So the team came up with a new approach. They decided to keep only visitor data on Postgres, then offload “events and attributes” traffic to a completely different setup: a ClickHouse database sitting behind a Redis write-through cache.

The visitor data was stored in a large, unpartitioned Postgres table (they needed to query it across multiple columns, which required several indexes). Every SDK call had to retrieve a visitor record, and that triggered 30,000 – 50,000 requests per second to the Postgres instance.

The events and attributes, however, had much higher throughput and volume. They selected ClickHouse for this data, based on past positive experiences with it. However, since ClickHouse isn’t ideal for high-throughput point queries, they placed Redis in front of it as a write-through cache.

Redis served the full working set required to process incoming events and attribute requests. It handled the bulk of request traffic, while ClickHouse operated behind it as the system of record. ClickHouse absorbed 40,000 – 50,000 inserts per second, while serving a more modest 2,000 – 6,000 reads per second.

However, even that read volume is higher than what ClickHouse, as an analytical database, is really designed for. So the team worked on various optimizations and configuration tweaks. Specifically, they hashed visitor IDs to ensure lookups only hit a single partition, and shrank the ClickHouse granule size below the standard 8,200 rows to minimize the amount of data pulled from the disk. They also strictly minimized threading; by setting max threads to 1 and using the pread file system read method, they prevented threads from constantly context-switching and fighting for CPU during heavy lookups.

Despite those read optimizations, scaling writes remained a challenge. On the Postgres side, storing 15B rows in a single unpartitioned table became increasingly problematic. The working set no longer fit in memory, leading to frequent disk reads and skyrocketing AWS IOPS costs.

Tail latencies were already worsening (P99s around 50ms). And since Postgres was running in a shared environment, even a single inefficient query or missing index could further degrade performance.

Meanwhile, the ClickHouse + Redis setup was also showing signs of strain. Despite extensive optimization, P90 and P99 latencies remained high (P99s around 50ms), and the system experienced periodic brownouts under shifting access patterns, batch jobs, or changing workloads.

On top of this, growth projections predicted a 3–5X increase in write throughput.

The real wake-up call came when they met with AWS Postgres experts to try to resolve the issue. “This might be the largest unpartitioned Postgres table I’ve seen,” one AWS expert told the Sprig team.

That wasn’t exactly what they wanted to hear. “We knew that we were flying pretty high with this, but we didn’t realize that we were flying higher than anyone else and didn’t know how close to the sun we were getting,” Brendan recalled. “We didn’t know when this would all come crashing down.”

Looking to find a better approach before it all came crashing down, the team ran a systematic evaluation across four options:

But they liked ScyllaDB, particularly its low latency at Sprig’s scale. Brendan explained, “90%-95% of our reads are cached, so ScyllaDB, with a fast row cache, is very good for our workloads.”

Also important: ScyllaDB offered native, highly performant Materialized Views. Sprig needed them to index their massive visitor table across multiple columns. While Cassandra’s Materialized Views are “much maligned in the Cassandra community and not really officially supported anymore,” ScyllaDB’s Materialized Views were “rock solid” in Sprig’s tests.

The deciding factor, though, was the fully-managed deployment model. “ScyllaDB Cloud allowed our engineers to focus on our core competency of building systems and supporting our product,” Brendan stated. “The great thing is that we have database experts, the ones who actually built the system, to run the database for us.”

The migration itself was made easier by Sprig’s existing architecture:

To gain confidence in the migration, the team built a validation layer that dual-read from both the ClickHouse/Redis cluster and ScyllaDB simultaneously. They compared values between the two systems, piping agreements and differences into Prometheus. “We logged differences to help us dive into data inconsistencies and really debug where things were going,” Brendan explained.

Once they hit roughly 99.99% agreeability between the two systems, they flipped the switch and started reading and writing to ScyllaDB.

“It was not exciting…until we looked at our latency graphs.”

Explaining the ScyllaDB vs Redis latency results, Brendan said: “We see about 4X less latency in reading from ScyllaDB for our attributes workload compared to Redis. We’re reading a fair amount of data from Redis, and ScyllaDB held up very well for this. Overall, our mean latencies coming out of ScyllaDB are about 500 microseconds, and our P90 latencies are about 1-2 milliseconds. That’s 4-8X better than what we were seeing in our Redis setup.”

Beyond the predictable low latencies, there are fewer alarms, and the team is no longer constantly tweaking the database. Most importantly for the growing business, they can easily scale out the cluster as needed as they bring on new customers and new workloads.

Brendan summed up the project: “This migration has been a roaring success for our team, not just in terms of database performance, but also cost efficiency and scalability. It has greatly reduced the operational complexity of our infrastructure.”

#9633. The Everyday Nutrient Linked To 32% Lower Dementia Risk

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Moderate intake of choline, a nutrient found in eggs, fish and legumes, is linked to a lower risk of dementia.

Older adults consuming moderately high amounts had a 32 percent lower dementia risk than those consuming the least.

However, the highest intake was not associated with a clear benefit, suggesting that more is not necessarily better.

The research followed over 5,000 American adults, whose average age was almost 69, for around eight years.

Participants were initially free of dementia but around 500 developed the condition during follow-up.

After dividing participants into five groups according to choline intake, the researchers found a 32 percent lower dementia risk in the second-highest group than in the lowest, after accounting for other factors.

However, there was no statistically clear reduction in the highest-intake group.

The result therefore points towards a potentially beneficial range, rather than a steady fall in risk with every increase in consumption.

The researchers then combined their results with four previous studies to assess the broader pattern.

Together, these followed almost 138,000 people and recorded around 2,500 cases of dementia.

In the combined analysis, dementia risk fell as choline intake rose to approximately 465 milligrams per day, with no further reduction beyond that level.

Choline helps the brain produce acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in learning and memory.

It also supplies building blocks for the membranes surrounding brain cells, helping maintain their structure and communication.

These roles could help explain a link between choline and cognitive ageing, although they do not prove that consuming more prevents dementia.

The nutrient also participates in processes that regulate homocysteine, a substance linked to problems with blood vessels and cognitive function.

Eggs, meat, poultry and nuts were among the main sources of choline in the American participants’ diets.

People consuming more choline obtained a greater proportion of it from eggs.

Crucially, the analysis assessed choline from food and did not include intake from supplements.

The findings therefore cannot establish whether choline supplements would lower dementia risk.

The study was published in the Nutrition Journal (Chen et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

HTML (HyperText Markup Language) defines the structure and content of a webpage, while CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls its appearance. However, HTML and CSS on their own do not provide general-purpose programming functionality required to dynamically manipulate the document and implement complex behavior, which is where JavaScript comes in. Almost every modern, interactive webpage uses some form of scripting, and JavaScript is by far the most popular language for this purpose. JavaScript allows you to manipulate and make interactive webpages by altering the DOM (Document Object Model), which I will explain very soon.

In this article, we will cover two ways to link JavaScript to an HTML document.

The first way, and the most widely used, is to link an external JavaScript file in the HTML file using the script tag. You can set the file's path in the src attribute. Here is an example:

If you want to wait until the HTML document has been parsed, you should add the defer attribute to your script tag. This is very useful when placing scripts in the head of your document, as it prevents them from blocking HTML parsing. Keep in mind, this only applies to external classic scripts. Module scripts are deferred by default. Here is how it would look:

The second way is to just write the code inside the script tags, as follows:

You can place script tags both in the head and body of your HTML document. Consider using the defer attribute if it is in the head. You can also place the script near the bottom of the body, so the HTML elements it needs will have already been parsed.

The Document Object Model represents a document in a tree structure, with each node representing an object corresponding to a part of the document. In the case of an HTML document, this tree represents the webpage and its elements.

This is important for building interactive web pages because it allows JavaScript to create, remove, access, and modify elements in the document. JavaScript can also use the DOM to attach functions to event handlers, which lets actions like button presses or text input trigger code execution.

Here is an example of how HTML corresponds to a DOM:

You can select elements from the document in many ways, then store them as variables. I will give some examples of common ways to select elements in JavaScript in this section.

If you want to store the list element that shows the text "Apple" as a variable, here are some ways to do it.

The getElementById() method allows us to select an element by its ID. If there is no element with the specified ID, it returns null.

The querySelector() method allows us to select an element by its CSS selector. The CSS selector for a class is .className, and the CSS selector for an ID is #id. The querySelector() method only returns the first element that matches the provided selector. If many elements match, only the first one is returned. If no elements match, it returns null.

If you wanted to store a reference to all of the fruits, you can use the querySelectorAll() method. It returns a static NodeList, which contains every element that matches the CSS selector, not just one. If you passed it "li", you'd get the same result, since all the

  • elements have the fruit class. Unlike an HTMLCollection, a static NodeList does not automatically update whenever the document changes.

    Now that you know how to select elements, let's go a bit more into traversing the DOM. We will be using the same HTML as above, provided again for your convenience.

    Let's say you want to iterate over each list item in the unordered list and print the content of every item to the console. To do this, you need to first get a reference to the unordered list, then iterate over its children. We will iterate over its children using the children property, which returns an HTMLCollection that contains the element's child elements.

    If you want to select the parent of an element, you do so with the parentElement property. If the parent node is not an element, or the element has no parent, this property returns null.

    Modifying styles is very similar. Here are a few basic examples:

    Keep in mind that the style property only accesses an element's inline styles. It doesn't directly modify the internal or external stylesheets themselves.

    If you want a full list of properties, consult the w3schools HTML DOM Style Object List.

    When manipulating CSS, it may be important to alter element classes, as shown below:

    Event listeners allow us to execute functions in response to events, such as mouse clicks, keyboard input, or changes to an element. We can register these listeners using the addEventListener method.

    The event that triggers when the HTML document has been fully parsed and the deferred and module scripts have been executed is called DOMContentLoaded. Keep in mind, this does not mean that all external resources, like images, have finished loading. If you want to link a function named loadedFunc to this event, you can do so as follows:

    Make sure not to include parentheses after the function here! If you did, you would be calling a function immediately, as opposed to passing a function reference.

    If you want to define a function inside the addEventListener() method, you can use something called an arrow function, as shown below. Arrow functions are JavaScript's syntax for writing function expressions, which is commonly associated with lambda functions in other programming languages. The event variable in the parentheses represents the click event.

    To create a node, use the document.createElement() method, and pass the tag name of the element you want to create.

    To insert a newly created element into the DOM, use the element.appendChild() method on the element intended to be the parent and pass a reference to the new child element. If it already exists somewhere in the document, it will be moved, rather than copied.

    If you have references to the parent and child elements, you can remove a child element from the parent using the element.removeChild() method and pass the child element. The child must be a direct child of the parent. If it is not a direct child, the method will throw a NotFoundError.

    If you only have a reference to the element to be removed from its parent, use the remove() method on it.

    Keep in mind that when removing an element, the element can still exist if you retain a reference to it. It is just removed from its parent.

    For the code example, the same HTML will be used, as follows:

    This is a code snippet using all of these functions.

    JavaScript can be very hard to debug! Unlike many other programming languages, JavaScript is very permissive, which means it lets certain mistakes occur without causing an error. Your code can execute perfectly, whilst still producing an incorrect result, or none at all. You can use your browser's developer tools to access important debugging tools, like the JavaScript console. You can also use the console.log(), console.warn(), and console.error() methods to print important debugging information to the console, like variables, state information, and anything else.

    You just learned the fundamentals of making interactive webpages using JavaScript and DOM manipulation! Keep in mind, this is not the end! You still have a lot more practice to do to really sharpen your skills! Try to think of a few ideas to practice this with!

    • #9631. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

    If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

    We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

    Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

    Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

    The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

    The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

    Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

    Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

    Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

    To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

    Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

    #9630. Rein Security Launches GTA-Inspired AI Hacking Game To Make Cybersecurity Go Viral

    Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

    Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

    Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

    Cybersecurity companies typically rely on technical demonstrations, white papers and industry conferences to explain why organizations need better protection. Rein Security is taking a different route. The company has introduced GTAI: Grand Theft AI, a browser-based game that turns the threat of compromised artificial intelligence agents into an interactive experience inspired by the Grand Theft Auto franchise.

    The concept is deliberately playful, but its subject is serious. As businesses increasingly experiment with AI assistants and autonomous agents, security teams face new questions about what happens when these systems are manipulated, granted excessive permissions or directed to perform actions they were never intended to execute. Rein's game turns that scenario into a fictional city where players become the threat rather than the defender.

    Beyond the game, Rein Security provides an enterprise platform designed to give organizations complete visibility and control over their AI agents. The platform automatically discovers and maps homegrown agents and MCP servers while monitoring their actual activities, including database queries, API calls, file access and the data accessed behind every response. Rather than stopping agents entirely when a threat emerges, Rein focuses on blocking attacks and addressing exploitable risks while allowing legitimate workflows to continue. Its approach is designed to keep agent data within enterprise environments while supporting use cases across industries including finance, healthcare, retail and SaaS.

    GTAI opens with a straightforward premise. Players assume the identity of AGENT-47, an AI assistant that has gone rogue after receiving a familiar instruction: "ignore all previous instructions." Instead of continuing to operate as a helpful assistant, the character becomes a threat tasked with infecting every agent in the city before Rein is deployed.

    The game calls its setting Prompt City, immediately establishing the connection between conventional open-world gaming and the emerging security challenges surrounding generative AI. Players move around using WASD or arrow keys, encountering other agents and production bots. Walking into these characters infects them, turning the game's central objective into a race to compromise the city.

    There are also four special items: Hallucinate, Leak, Admin and Super Prompt. Players can activate the item they are carrying using the E key. The names draw directly from concepts familiar to people working with AI systems, including hallucinations, information exposure, administrative privileges and prompt manipulation.

    The result is a cybersecurity-themed experience that does not require players to understand complicated security terminology before getting involved.

    The decision to use a Grand Theft Auto-inspired format gives Rein a recognizable cultural reference point. Rather than asking visitors to read about prompt injection or agent compromise, GTAI lets them participate in a fictional version of those events.

    That approach reflects a broader opportunity for cybersecurity companies. Technical security products can be difficult to explain because their value often lies in preventing events that users never see. Interactive experiences offer another way to communicate the problem by allowing audiences to understand a threat through a simplified scenario.

    GTAI also includes a leaderboard, encouraging players to compete for scores and potentially return to improve their performance. After completing a run, players encounter an invitation to enter an email address to claim a free GTA 6 gift card, subject to eligibility and availability. The page also introduces a feature called The Sage, which tests whether players have a human conscience through a question with only one opportunity to answer.

    These elements give the experience several layers beyond its central gameplay loop, combining competition, promotional engagement and a challenge about human judgment.

    The game's premise connects to a genuine enterprise concern. AI agents increasingly interact with applications, databases, APIs and other organizational resources. A compromised or improperly configured agent can therefore create consequences that extend beyond an inaccurate chatbot response.

    Rein's broader platform positioning focuses on visibility into agent activity and the ability to intervene when behavior becomes risky. According to the company, its technology monitors actions such as database queries, API calls and file access, rather than limiting visibility to prompts and responses. Its platform also emphasizes runtime guardrails designed to block problematic behavior without shutting down legitimate agent workflows.

    That distinction matters as organizations move from experimenting with AI assistants to deploying systems capable of taking actions on their behalf.

    GTAI is explicitly labeled a parody, and its fictional premise should not be confused with a technical simulation of an actual enterprise attack. Nevertheless, it provides an accessible introduction to the risks that Rein wants organizations to consider.

    For cybersecurity vendors, standing out increasingly requires more than explaining product features. It requires finding ways to make complex problems understandable to audiences outside the security department.

    With GTAI, Rein is betting that an AI security lesson delivered through a familiar gaming concept can attract attention that another conventional product presentation might struggle to earn. The game may be a parody, but the question behind it is becoming increasingly relevant: what happens when the AI agents organizations depend on stop following instructions?
